speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rather than make a speech concerning my riding, which has many problems,

I am going to discuss one of the several national problems facing the Canadian people which I think should be brought to their attention. Canada is faced today with two major problems. One is unemployment and the other is inflation. In this debate my colleagues have offered to the government some advice in solving the rising unemployment situation. I should like to do the same with respect to inflation. That this problem is important was illustrated by the words of James Muir, president of the Royal Bank of Canada, when he said:
We seem to have reached the economists' hell on earth; inflation and unemployment. The alternately "creeping" and "surging" inflation is apparently still the pattern in recovery as well as in recession. I believe that this chronic inflation is the greatest single threat to Canada's economic development. The disease must be studied, it must be understood, and it must be cured.
I was very pleased to hear that the previous speaker has considered this matter and has offered some suggestions to solve the problem. Economists in general are very concerned over the present economy of Canada which is seeing for the first time in history both inflation and unemployment. Previously it was felt that inflation would end unemployment, and many economists today are trying to find what, change has taken place that produces this phenomenon.
The question can legitimately be asked, what is inflation? One opinion was advanced by Mr. D. E. Kilgour, vice president and managing director of the Great West Life Assurance Company who, when speaking in Montreal, said:
Inflation is simply a technique of stealing money without the embarrassment of identifying the victim or too closely pointing out the benefactors. One thing is abundantly clear. It is that insurance policyholders are being victimized and also the holders of savings accounts, bonds and pensions. If this generation has not the fortitude or the wisdom or the restraint to control the grab-bag of inflation, we can destroy our democratic nations and our way of life.
Or, as was said on another occasion by Gladstone Murray:
An honest dollar is the noblest work of government; an inflated dollar is the vilest.
Canada today has reason to show concern about the problem of inflation. Inflation is considered to be an essential element in a capitalist economy. An increasing labour force, technological advance and automation make it necessary to increase industrial production continually. Otherwise rapidly developing unemployment cannot be avoided.
It is estimated that a 5 per cent annual increase in industrial expansion must have a monetary inflation of from 1 to 2 per cent per annum to maintain such expansion. Therefore a capitalist economy cannot have both

full employment and a stable currency. This was realized by the people of the country when the Bank of Canada was established, because in the preamble to the Bank of Canada Act we find these words:
Whereas it is desirable to establish a central bank in Canada to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation, to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment, so far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action, and generally to promote the economic and financial welfare of the dominion-
That is taken from the 1956 annual report by Mr. Coyne. He goes on to indicate that each country is responsible for its own inflationary pressures where they exist. He states on page 4 of the same book that although most countries in the western world experienced a measure of inflation this was chiefly due to causes within each country and manifested itself more in costs of production and distribution than in raw material prices.	After maintaining that
some of these inflationary factors should be controlled by the federal government, he points out on page 5 of the report that "the so-called federal credit controls do not exist". He goes on further to indicate the fields in which they do not exist, referring particularly to finance companies operating without the controls which governments can and do exercise with regard to questions of interest and related matters.
With a steady increase in industrial development during the past century, the value of our dollar has continued to fall. Today the value of the Canadian dollar is less than half its prewar value in terms of purchasing power. Let us review what has happened to the economy of Canada in the last 20 years.
For the first six years, 1939 to 1945, under a partly planned economy, by the use of price controls implemented during the war inflation was very moderate especially when one considers the huge expansion that took place during those six years. By 1945, the end of the war, the Canadian people had accumulated a fantastic volume of purchasing power. This had been accomplished by the purchasing of war bonds, service gratuities and other methods of compulsory savings. All types of consumer goods were in short supply. It was obvious that if the wartime price controls were removed this great power in the hands of consumers to buy goods which were in short supply would result in severe inflation. The Canadian Manufacturers Association and other organizations with similar interests persuaded three of the political parties in Canada to 66968-9-31
The Address-Mr. Peters press for the removal of these controls. The C.C.F. alone warned of the potential dangers to the stability of our currency and our economy.
However, the Canadian people who had at such great sacrifice saved their money now wished to purchase the consumer goods they had been unable to purchase for many years. The manufacturers, taking advantage of the short supply, boosted prices as high as the traffic would bear. We all know the disastrous results to the purchasing power of the dollar which occurred in the years immediately following the end of the war.
What is the situation today? The whole theory that the one and only cause of inflation is too much money chasing too few goods, causing a rise in prices, is no longer true. This theory was based on the premise that our economy would allow prices to find their own level. This theory is no longer true in practice, because today we see prices continuing to rise in the face of unemployment and a scarcity of money among a large segment of our population.
We contend that our problem should no longer be called "inflation" but rather "rising prices". We no longer have a situation where prices are mainly determined by the cost of production or demand and controlled within limits by the element of competition. Prices today are determined to an alarming extent by corporations, monopolies and cartels which, though less in number, are growing rapidly in size. This is especially true in the fields of basic materials; for example, in the price of steel, automobiles and energy. The determining factor in the setting of a price now is what the traffic will bear.
We in the C.C.F. wholeheartedly agree with the recent request by the Canadian Labour Congress for an immediate public investigation into the automobile, steel, farm implement and other basic industries. The congress is also to be commended for its demands on the government to strengthen the effectiveness of the Combines Investigation Act.
The people of Canada have a right to know if the reputed benefits to the consumer from competition are still available. The people of Canada are desirous of having a real investigation made so that they can determine whether or not there is any relationship between labour costs and retail prices. Statistics are available by the score to prove to us that both wages and prices are rising independently of each other.
In Canada today a concerted effort is being made to make labour the scapegoat

The Address-Mr. Peters in an attempt to avoid discovering what are the real causes which produce rising prices. Let us examine, for example, the increase in wages compared with productivity for the years from 1947 to 1955. On page 397 of the publication "Output, Labour and Capital in the Canadian Economy" the author warns us that the productivity figures are at best to be regarded as rough estimates, but adds that these are the best figures available. The figures do not indicate that wages have increased over productivity, which, if it had been the case, might have been a cause of our postwar inflation. On the contrary, these figures suggest that wages have been slightly lower than the increase in productivity. This would tend to contradict completely the statements of the manufacturers association, newspapers and financial publications that increases in wages are responsible for the high cost of living. For this period, 1947 to 1955, productivity in manufacturing rose by 32.12 per cent and real wage rates by only 30.51 per cent.
It should be noted in fairness to labour that unions have sought increases which they were able to justify to conciliation boards and public opinion as only maintaining the standard of living that their employees had previously enjoyed. In many cases the demands of labour, based on the cost of living at the time of current negotiations are met many months and sometimes years after the cost of living has continued to rise, so that the worker finds after obtaining a wage increase that he has not been able to maintain his standard of living.
Mr. Graham Towers, former governor of the Bank of Canada, said the same thing a great deal more briefly on November 14, 1957, in a speech on inflation which he made at a joint meeting of the life underwriters' association of Toronto and the Toronto chapter of the institute of chartered life underwriters. This is what Mr. Towers said:
Current discussions of inflation often refer to it as the "cost-push" type; and as labour is a very important factor in costs, price-increases more often than not are attributed to the successful efforts of labour unions to secure wage increases greater than increases in output per man hour. Labour, quite properly, I think, resents being saddled with a large share of the blame for the lower value of money. They are certaintly not responsible to any greater degree than all the rest of the population for what occurred during and immediately after the two world wars. It is not worth while to argue about the extent to which increases in wages in excess of increases in the productivity of labour have contributed to the rise in the cost of living during the last year and a half.
Organized labour, operating in our modern society, has an obligation to its membership to try and maintain the standard of living enjoyed by its membership. The Prime

Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) was, in my opinion, unfair when he addressed the Canadian Labour Congress convention in Winnipeg and asked them to hold the line on wages while at the same time making no effort to preach restraint to the other segments of our economy.
Mr. Towers pointed out that leaders of government have appealed for restraint on a number of occasions in the United States and the United Kingdom. Such appeals resulted in a growing awareness on the part of the public, but produced no tangible results.
The willingness of big business to cooperate with labour for the general economic good was clearly indicated in the United States when Walter Reuther, president of the united automobile workers, offered to maintain, or even lower, the wages enjoyed by his membership if the automobile industry would reduce the price of their cars to the consumer by $200. He was told to mind his own business, to run his union, and they would run their companies. The subsequent strike of 150,000 General Motors' employees obtained a sizeable increase based on maintaining the current standard of living which resulted in the wage increase plus interest being passed on to the consumer. In application, a wage increase is desirable to big business which operates, in the main, on the principle of cost of production plus a predetermined mark-up or profit. The higher the cost, the higher the profit. An example is Massey-Harris who in the ten-year period, according to the Financial Post, was able to increase its profits by 254 per cent.
Agriculture and agricultural leaders speak of the cost-price squeeze and it is an undesirable condition where the cost of the production rises while the selling price of the product remains the same or, in most cases, continues to fall.
Labour denies that wages are the deciding factor in our rising prices spiral. They contend that prices are rising because of other factors over which they have no control. The workers of Canada have no alternative but to join together with their fellow workers in order to protect themselves against the system under which we live. Many statistics are available to prove the returns to labour are only in line with increased production and are always lagging behind prices. Statistics are also available to prove that the non-labour part of retail prices has risen more rapidly than wage prices. The worst offender in the non-labour price rise has been the profit element. Just taking one example that appeared during the steelworkers' strike of local 1005, it was pointed out that the Steel Company of Canada had increased its net

profits alter taxes in the ten year period from 1946 to 1956 by 790 per cent while at the same time the average weekly wages had increased by only 60 per cent.

Savings in banks have been hit, as I said. This is something to which the

The Address-Mr. Peters government must give consideration. Certainly all the leaders of banking institutions are considering the implications of inflation and now it is time for the government of the country to do something about the matter. Because costs have risen in the matter of food, shelter and clothing, pensioners of all kinds are undergoing great difficulty. In these three basic commodities the rise in the cost of living has been greater than in any other field, and certainly this matter of inflation has taken its toll on the savings and the pensions of the Canadian people.
I have attempted, Mr. Speaker, to show that since the days of the industrial revolution, either inflation or unemployment has plagued our society. Today Canada is faced with both inflation and unemployment for the first time. Indeed, the only time we had a relatively stable currency and full employment was when we were at war and had a planned economy. The problem today, with the disappearance of free enterprise and competition, is really one of rising prices and not of inflation as we used to know the term. Today corporations, monopolies and cartels, with tremendous powers are determining prices on the principle of what the traffic will bear. The activities of these powerful forces need to be curtailed, in that they must be prepared to act primarily in the public interest. This control of those who exploit our human and natural resources must be supplemented by control of those who deal with currency and credit within our country. We feel that the measures we propose are essential for the health of our own economy and are also essential to the interests of the free world in general and the needs of mankind.
Unless these concepts are adopted, real confidence cannot be restored in the hearts of Canadians. Uncertainty, indecision and floundering can be disastrous and can lead us to chaos. Mere palliatives will, at least, lead only to brief periods of rapid expansion and flash-in-the-pan prosperity. Those responsible for government must analyze what has happened over the past century and also consider the vast changes which have taken place within the last generation. Such an analysis must then be followed up by long range policies. Only in this way can real confidence and prosperity be given to our people. There is a growing body of responsible, well-informed and thinking people which is rapidly coming to the conclusion that parliament and government, and especially this parliament and this government, must assume responsibility for the economic welfare of our nation and of our people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to rise on this ninth day of this debate and take part and follow some of the distinguished members who have already made their contributions. Before I begin I would like to join with other members in offering my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for Provencher, who gave such a clear account of the problems of the prairie farmers and of agriculture in general and the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet who made such a strong and sincere plea for the rights of the individual no matter to what race or religion he might belong. I think it is important for us to remember that our belief in one Canada is stronger than all the things which may have helped to divide us in the past.
To you, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say how extremely pleased we all are to see your return to the chair. You have always discharged your duties with dignity and impartiality and you have thus gained the respect of each and every member in this house. The same remarks apply to the Deputy Speaker.
This is the second parliament which I have attended as the member for the constituency of Renfrew South. During this time I have had the opportunity to compare the throne speeches of this government with those of the previous regime and I am particularly impressed with the content of this throne speech. Outlined in this speech is the confidence which our Prime Minister (Mr. Dief-enbaker) and his cabinet and the supporters of this government have in the men and women of Canada. Put briefly, the throne speech is a vote of confidence in Canada and in the Canadian people. It was once sufficient for a government to make a few platitudinous statements about our canals and the state of our economy. Today we are concerned with our whole country, with the welfare of our fellow Canadians and with the broad aspects of human relations between our people everywhere, yes, and with Canada's role in a world where time and distance are being shrunk in ratio to the increased speed of communication.
Canada, as we know, borders the two most powerful nations in the world today, namely the United States of America and the Union

of Soviet Socialist Republics. This is a geographical fact, and if we ignore the responsibility our position as a middle power entails, then we shall be doing a great disservice both to ourselves and to the other peace-loving nations of the world. We as a nation have confidence in each other and in the other nations that with us are seeking a lasting peace in the world today. I believe that without that trust and confidence in each other none of us can live in freedom and security.
A few days ago the Leader of the Opposition spoke about the state of the Canadian economy. I was struck with the substance of his remarks which showed a woeful lack of confidence in both his country and the men and women who live in it. For years the members of the former government, now in opposition, clung to the 49th parallel with a sort of ostrich-like blindness. When they did lift their eyes they always seemed to be facing south, seeking help from our neighbours. Their lack of faith held us all, or most of us, bound to the settled portions of our country.
This is now changing through the government's national development policy. The members of our government have told the people of this country that we have faith in the future of Canada. We have chosen to identify ourselves with the men and women who are showing the courage and the foresight to move north and to take their chances in the vast and challenging new areas which are being developed. We do not believe that it is the duty of our neighbours to the south of us to show us how to develop our own country. We believe that if we are to have sovereignty over the thousands of square miles of our northland, then we as Canadians must go there and live, and Canadians are doing just that. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) deserves special credit for the initiative and enterprise he and his department have shown in this regard.
I have mentioned these matters because our friends across the way are more accustomed to dealing in division than in the strength of unity. When they speak they still show that they lack confidence in the very people they represent, the men and women of Canada. They do not want to recognize the responsibility of leadership and the playing of their role of opposition; they are more concerned with the negative view of opposition than with the positive role of constructive criticism. They still suffer from the complex of defeat and they are still tempted to blame the Canadian people for that defeat rather than their own shortcomings.
The Address-Mr. Baskin
Many have been the achievements of this government since it took office. Of great concern to each and every member of this government has been employment-and I emphasize "employment"-dollars in the working man's pocket. The government cannot look after every field of employment but this government has been able actively to promote construction across Canada. I would like to put on the record at this time a few facts that were outlined at the Canadian construction convention held in Montreal last week. I quote H. J. Ball, the retiring president of the association. The headline in the paper reads:
Many healthy developments in 1958.
The article reads:
Construction tops $7 billion.
Mr. Ball goes on to say:
The trend towards larger construction programs should continue in 1959, with a total of perhaps $7.5 billion.
A total of $7.5 billion of construction means the employment of over 625,000 Canadians in construction operations and an even greater number manufacturing, transporting and merchandising construction materials and equipment or supplying services dependent upon construction activity. It will mean that over one out of every five dollars spent in Canada in end goods and services will be a construction dollar.
In 1958, while all this construction of new homes was taking place, there were over 150,000 units completed, the biggest homebuilding boom in Canada's history, and 1959 promises to be just as good. What impetus will this building boom have on our immediate future? Once again our factories are commencing to hum, our manufacturers are busy and will be much busier. Heavy industrial machinery, new stoves, refrigerators, washing machines and furniture will be required. My colleague, the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) advises me that for the first time in many years the furniture factories in his riding are operating on an overtime basis.
I have just mentioned the 150,000 houses completed last year in Canada. We all know that this is a direct result of the action taken by this government in amending the National Housing Act to provide an additional amount of $350 million. My home county of Renfrew was able to obtain from this fund the sum of $1,615,922, and from our banks and loans companies an additional amount of $649,000. These sums provided 231 new housing units in our area. Over and above this, our Department of Public Works has awarded contracts in Renfrew county for approximately 500 units having a total value of $6,137,800. The Department of Defence Production is presently processing tenders for a new $1 million

The Address-Mr. Baskin project near Eganville in my riding. This project will be under way early in February, and it will involve a considerable labour force. A great deal of material will be required, material which is manufactured in the district. Our carpenters, bricklayers, plumbers, electricians and, in fact, all tradesmen can look forward to a more prosperous year.
In so far as hospital construction is concerned, we plan to spend in the coming year more than $2 million. This will include a new 32-bed hospital at Barrys Bay, to be named the St. Francis memorial and district hospital. It will serve the western area of Renfrew county, a portion of Nipissing and part of the adjoining ridings of Hastings and Hastings-Frontenac. The estimated cost is in the neighbourhood of $400,000. There will be a three-quarters of a million dollar addition to the Arnprior and district memorial hospital and a one million dollar addition to the Victoria hospital in Renfrew. This new hospital construction is a direct result of the action taken by this government when they doubled the hospital construction grants early in 1958. A great deal of credit is due to our Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) for the role he played in the introduction of this legislation.
The Canadian civil defence college at Arnprior, Ontario, comes within the jurisdiction of our Minister of National Health and Welfare. There are about 100 men and women employed at this college and during the past year 3,524 Canadian citizens received training at the college. Citizens from across Canada who have trained at this college, and the citizens of the town of Arnprior and district, are indeed grateful to our government for the rebuilding in 1958 of the road that leads to the college. All of this is a direct result of the boldness, the imagination and foresight of this government. We have not been able to cure everything in Canada since we took office, but we have swung the economic pendulum in an upward turn.
The hon. gentlemen in the opposition want to remember just how fast we were heading towards a serious depression in late 1956 and early 1957 when they were swept out of office. There are those of you who will not admit it, but the Canadian people knew what was going on, and that is why you were voted out of office. You had become all too powerful, and had long since forgotten that you were the servants of the people and not their masters.
Returning to my constituency, I should like to note that our manufacturing firms greatly appreciate the co-operation they have received


from the various departments in our government, especially the Department of Defence Production, the Department of Transport and the Post Office Department. These manufacturing plants are keenly interested in our government's aircraft and missile program. They are hopeful of participating in the manufacture of equipment which is to be installed on the proposed new guided missile sites in northern Quebec and northern Ontario.
My people were greatly concerned over the fact that Canadian National Railways made application last November to the board of transport commissioners for the discontinuance of the railway passenger service between Ottawa and Barrys Bay. The board met in Pembroke with all interested officials and citizens concerned. Following a two-day hearing, the application of the Canadian National was not approved. The discontinuance of this service would have completely shut off a section of the people in our county. I am pleased to say that the Canadian National Railways is now in the process of instituting a new and modern service. I wish to say to our Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) how very much our Renfrew county citizens appreciate the decision of the commissioners, and through him I wish to thank them.
Television reception is not satisfactory in many areas of the riding I represent. This is particularly true of the Eganville area and westward to Barrys Bay, Madawaska and Whitney which is on the borderline of Algonquin park. The government and the C.B.C. are very much aware of this situation because I have made numerous representations about it during the past year and a half. I have made these representations, not only to our Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) but also through him to the general manager of the C.B.C. Our people in Renfrew South, of course, realize that the same situation prevails in many other areas of Canada. I am pleased to say that this year a number of new low-power transmitters will be installed to correct this situation, and I have been advised that better reception will prevail in my constituency in the not too distant future.
There has been a need in all sections of Canada for new postal services and extensions to existing services. I wish to commend the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) and his entire department for the vigorous action they have taken to improve the postal service generally across this country. Renfrew South, which I represent, covers a large rural area and at the time this government took office in June, 1957 many of my constituents were dissatisfied with the rural mail situation. At that time the density requirement throughout the rural areas of Canada was

four householders per mile. In a number of areas in my riding, as well as elsewhere in Canada, citizens were not receiving daily mail because the density of householders along many of the concessions was less than four per mile. The change in the density regulation has meant new rural routes and extensions to existing routes. Ninety-two new routes have been established and some 1,700 extensions authorized, serving approximately 40,000 additional patrons.
Householders served by rural routes and suburban services now total over 600,000. I know that the people deeply appreciate this improved service. We have not completely corrected the situation, and will not until the density requirement is reduced to two householders per mile. I have brought this to the attention of our Postmaster General. I believe that we have a Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) whose sympathies lie in this direction and that perhaps action will be forthcoming in this regard.
These are some of the things that are going on in my constituency and elsewhere in Canada. I have mentioned these construction projects, all of which have been made possible through the co-operation of the various cabinet ministers and the hardworking civil service in their respective departments. When you multiply this many times -and I know we have 208 members on this side of the house who are extremely active in this regard-you have some idea of the amount of effort that is being put into new development in this country under the leadership of a new and vigorous government.
For the future we are hopeful of increasing in my riding iron ore production in the townships of Bagot and Blythfleld, near Cala-bogie. The first few carloads of ore were mined there in December. It is hoped that full scale production will soon make this development an important part of our economy.
These accomplishments are not the work of any one individual. They represent the work and co-operation of many people. They also reflect the confidence of men and women in their government. Here I should like to say something about that confidence and the leadership that inspires it. When hon. members opposite or some of them were in office they were happy to think themselves supermen or at least they became known as such; but events have served to show them as something considerably less. The government which is now in office does not claim to be made up of supermen. But one great difference exists between it and the hon. members opposite. I refer to the leadership that these men and women are giving to this country. Particularly I should like to
The Address-Mr. Baskin speak of the Prime Minister who, I believe, has made his greatest contribution in the field to which I referred a little while ago, namely that of confidence in his fellow Canadians and in the future of this country.
On December 30 last he was interviewed by the Christian Science Monitor. I have the Christian Science Monitor and I wish to quote from it. When the Prime Minister was asked the question, what is Canada's most significant development today, he answered as follows:
Surely it is this dynamic new concept of Canadian-ism. It is a feeling of unity, and it is a sense of destiny, an awareness of what Canada can contribute in this churning world.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is the kind of positive, hopeful statement that the Prime Minister of Canada should be making to the world today. There is nothing boastful about this statement, nor is it one calculated to frighten other nations. Rather, I believe it is a statement made by a distinguished Canadian who, along with other members of his party, has an awareness of the important position his country must play as a bridge between nations.
In this respect I should like to refer to the commonwealth trade and economic conference held in Montreal last September. The scope of their deliberations was as broad as the diversity in interests of those who gathered around the conference table. Yet while the delegates at Montreal represented countries at every stage of economic development, every colour, culture and creed, they met not as strangers but as members of the same family. It is noteworthy that the theme of the conference was "an expanding commonwealth in an expanding world economy". The opposition may try as they will to downgrade the importance of this conference, but their criticism and their attitude are seen for their true worth when contrasted with the evaluation of the success of the conference made unanimously by the representatives of the commonwealth countries who participated. At the conclusion of the conference Right Hon. Derick Heathcoat Amory, Chancellor of the Exchequer, had this to say:
In the opinion of us all, I ana sure the results of our work here have amply justified the bold initiative of your Prime Minister, Mr. Diefenbaker, in proposing this conference a year ago. Looking ahead, it was hard to visualize that we would be able to cover so much ground and to reach so many decisions of great importance to our commonwealth aim of expansion and prosperity.
Before leaving this subject, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention the role of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). The success of the commonwealth trade and economic conference was in no small measure due to the

The Address-Mr. Baskin outstanding leadership given the deliberations at Montreal by the Minister of Finance.
On Wednesday, January 21, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), when he rose to take part in this debate, referred to the period of our history between the years 1867 and 1896. He reminded us of the spirit of confidence and optimism demonstrated by that great Conservative, Sir John A. Macdonald, the man who brought forth confederation and who was instrumental in the building of the C.P.R. which linked all Canada together. It is my belief that our party has never lost that spirit. I also feel that this same spirit was prevalent in the house last week when the Minister of Transport announced that Canadian Pacific Air Lines had been given the right to operate a daily service from Montreal to Vancouver. This announcement means that not only is Canada linked from coast to coast by two major air lines but that the passengers will be able to fly across this country and to other cities of the world without changing aircraft. This action, is significant of our optimism for the future and a further development by the government of Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker.
The Leader of the Opposition, a few days ago, spoke in terms of "ruin, confusion and doubt". It seems to me that his words, if they reflected anything, reflected the temper of his own party. I am certain that the majority of the Canadian people would not agree with him. Most of them are too busy earning a living, educating their children and carrying out their responsibilities as citizens to take this kind of wishful pessimism seriously.
To me, the future of this country appears to be extremely bright. The population by 1970 is quite likely to be at least 30 million. This means work and prosperity. It seems to me that opposition members should stop reading in Hansard old speeches of the years 1931, 1932 and 1933 and then getting up and repeating them as they have done during this debate. In my opinion this country is headed for no depression. Rather, it is headed in the opposite direction. We are on our way up.
For too long now the opposition have shown enthusiasm for only one subject, namely unemployment. Actually, Mr. Speaker, from the way in which they dwell upon it you would think that they had invented it. As far as we on this side of the house are concerned, we are doing our best to get rid of it. Whether hon. members opposite like it or not, they are going to have to find a new theme to replace unemployment, because once again Canada is marching forward 

steadily and assuredly. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the members of this government, placed here by the people of Canada, are finding an answer to the recession and to the problems bequeathed to them by those members who sit in gloomy judgment upon themselves across the way.

Mr. Speaker,
may I first of all express my congratulations to you upon the high position you occupy in this house. Although I have just had the pleasure of meeting you for the first time this session, I know that you have those fine qualities of tact, diplomacy, patience and good humour which fit you so admirably for the position you now hold.
Second, Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on their very creditable launching of this debate. Their contribution is recognized and appreciated. I hope also that my three hon. friends who were introduced at the opening of this session will find their work as challenging, interesting and rewarding as I have.
Third, Mr. Speaker, may I express through you to the electors of Trinity my gratitude for the honour they have given me. I received support from men and women of every race, colour and creed, people of varied backgrounds who all believe in the British parliamentary system and who felt it was imperative at this time that the people of metropolitan Toronto have a voice in the opposition. I appreciate their confidence and I assure them that I will do my utmost to prove worthy of the trust that has been shown. I regret the circumstances which made the byelection necessary and wish to join those who have paid tribute to the late Mr. Lockyer. He was a fine gentleman who received a great mandate last March. I join in the expressions of sympathy to Mrs. Lockyer.
There are many serious and urgent problems facing us at this time. I feel a bit sorry for the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his government but actually most of the problems are of their own making. Now they must face the difficult task of finding solutions. Among the most pressing of the problems are unemployment, inflation and defence. I intend to leave my remarks on the subject of defence until another time and to consider today the joint problems of unemployment and inflation and later, as it relates to them, the matter of trade.
I must, of course, talk about unemployment. It is something that affects tens of thousands of my fellow Torontonians. I have had the experience of learning about this problem in

terms of people rather than in terms of statistics. On the subject of statistics, however, I know that quite a number of people seeking work in Toronto are not registered with the national employment service and consequently the figures we get do not include all the people seeking work. One family I visited, a family of five, had no income, no money, a very sick boy in bed, three prescriptions from the doctor and no money to fill the prescriptions. Another man and his wife were living in one room without food and without adequate fuel for their stove. There are many other cases of equal hardship, and one cannot possibly come in direct contact with people living in these conditions without rebelling against a situation which permits such a thing.
This is not an underdeveloped country without sufficient resources to supply the basic needs of our people. It is a land of riches and it is not right that we should have so much poverty and distress in the shadow of plenty. It is not necessary to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the unemployment problem is twice as grievous now as it was under the former administration. This has been said many times and will be repeated until corrective action becomes effective. Not only do we have more people unemployed and for longer periods of time but these same people are being penalized through inflation. The prices of the things they need to keep body and soul together are rising and getting even farther beyond their reach. Unemployment insurance and relief payments buy even less of the necessities of life and prove quite inadequate for sustained periods. It is not good enough to say that we had inflation under the previous administration. The inflation of the immediate post-war period and the Korean era were caused by trying to do too much in too short a time, by overtaxing the physical capacity of the Canadian economy. The inflation of today is of an entirely different sort. We now have unused resources and hundreds of thousands of unemployed workers. Inflation under these circumstances cannot be condoned. It is a disease, an insidious, cancerous growth which eats at the very foundation of our economic system. It must be stopped before confidence in our currency is destroyed.
We were told that the reconversion loan of last year was designed to help control inflation. Until that contention is proven some of us may be forgiven for the notion that is was more inflationary than otherwise. At least the cost of borrowing is up, municipal taxes are up, federal taxes will have to go up or deficits increase, and the cost of 66968-9-32

speechtext:
Be patient. The extent of the deterioration makes the problem all the more complex but none the less real.
The government has launched a program of public works as its solution. It is a well known fact that public works are no solution at all. The effect on employment is delayed and the number of persons employed is very small in relation to the vast expenditure. No, Mr. Speaker, public works, other than those of a self-liquidating nature which generate additional employment, are not an answer. The answer is trade, domestic and international. It is interesting to note the interrelation between domestic and international trade. When international trade declines, domestic activity seems to follow suit. Likewise when international trade increases, domestic output increases together with employment.
What has been the government's position on trade? The British made a proposal. It was an obvious attempt on the part of the British government to encourage trade and increase the volume of transactions between our two countries to the advantage of each. Was it given serious consideration? Apparently not. It seems to have been summarily dismissed by the Minister of Finance. Surely, we should give serious consideration to such a forward-looking and liberal proposal. If not, the British are likely to view with scepticism the pious pronouncements of the Prime Minister and his ministers during the election campaign.
According to the newspapers, the British West Indies Federation has suggested a customs union with Canada. Our products are complementary, and the immediate acceptance of their proposal would likely result in nothing but benefit to each. It is strange that there has not been a single word from the government on this proposal either.
In short, the government's reaction to trade has been the traditional Conservative one of running up trade barriers with the inevitable consequence of lower business activity and greater unemployment. In addition to urging the government to reconsider the British proposal and to consider seriously the one from the British West Indies, I wish to put forward a few broader suggestions about how it would be possible to increase international trade. I must make it clear that
(Mr. Hellyer.]
the proposals I intend to outline, although strictly liberal in nature, have not been considered by my colleagues and, consequently, are presented as my own views.
I am a convinced and unrepentant free trader. Oh, I fully appreciate the impossibility of achieving a world without tariff barriers overnight, but I believe it is a goal to be sought. The recent pronouncements of the soviet leaders that they intend to outstrip the west must be taken seriously. Undoubtedly in the world struggle in which we are engaged the soviet will bend every effort to equal and, if possible, to surpass us in the fields of military preparedness and domestic production and trade. Whether they are successful or not depends on ourselves. To keep our front, the western world must expand production and trade in each of its component parts. We must have something better than we now have. Surely a system which permits 10 per cent or more of the available labour force to sit in idleness needs to be streamlined. These conditions are not good enough to merit support at home or acceptance by the uncommitted nations abroad. We cannot casually accept the existence of poverty, misery and hardship in a society which claims to be affluent. One of the great mechanics available to us in the pursuit of expansion is increased trade.
The Liberal party should be complimented on its effort to expand trade since world war II. The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade has been a noble experiment and has undoubtedly encouraged a higher level of international trade than would have been possible without it. Canada has been a world leader in its efforts to make the agreement work and has always-at least until quite recently-tried to live up to the spirit and the letter of that agreement. The great weakness of GATT has been the fact that the intent and spirit could be frustrated and to a degree made ineffective by customs regulations and interpretation.
Let us consider, as an example, the trading relations between Canada and the United States. I have seldom heard a red-blooded Canadian manufacturer admit or infer that he could not meet United States competition on equal terms. All most manufacturers ask is the same access to United States markets that his United States competitor has to the Canadian market. Unfortunately for many products and industries such has not been the case. It has been because of this one-sided aspect of trade and the frustration of trying to do business with the United States within the terms of its customs regulations which have caused many people to appear to reject the principle of free trade and to fall back

upon the old cry for protectionism. This is a most unfortunate effect and tends to divert attention from the real principles involved.
On the subject of what trade really accomplishes, the Conservative and Liberal approaches are opposite. Let us consider for a moment the position of the people living on the Japanese islands. They have to trade to live. They literally cannot produce enough food domestically to keep themselves from starvation. They must exchange manufactured products for food. The moral answer to this problem is clear enough. If we believe in the brotherhood of man we must accept responsibility for our fellow mortals. We must not just allow, but actively help these people to earn a livelihood. Any other course would be inhuman and certainly unchristian. If we fail we drive them to the point of desperation where they have only two alternatives-starvation, or a war of aggression, or self-preservation, depending upon one's point of view.
The economic answer is not as clear, nor as universally agreed. The Conservative views the import of Japanese manufacturers as a direct threat. The goods imported and consumed in Canada cause the unemployment of those Canadians who would otherwise have produced an equal volume of the same merchandise. The Liberal does not look on the import as an isolated transaction. The Liberal knows that every dollar earned by the Japanese for their manufactures comes right back to Canada, most of it for wheat and barley. The farmer receiving the income from his grain decides to buy a new car or a new tractor. The automobile or implement manufacturer buys tires, accessories and other components for his product, and on it goes. Trade is a chain reaction. When trade is expanding, income and employment expand. When trade contracts, business slows down and bread lines grow.
I should not like to imply that there are not some specific industries that feel the pinch from specific imports. There are some, but actually, in most cases, it is not an entire industry but specific products of an industry which face stiff competition from abroad. The loudest objections come from industries where the management is inflexible and not aware of the possibility of new products and new markets.
Taking our great industrial complex as a whole, one concludes that it would benefit from expanded trade and this benefit would be reflected in higher profits and greater employment. How then can we achieve the goal of increased trade within our terms of reference, the real world in which we live? I think the present General Agreement on 66968-9-32J
The Address-Mr. Hellyer Tariffs and Trade which has served its purpose and been a useful experiment should not be renewed. Such a radical proposal could not be made, of course, without an alternative proposal which is more likely to accomplish the desired result.
I would beg to suggest, therefore, that instead of renewing the present agreement that a new one be negotiated along the following lines. Each signatory nation would agree to two schedules of tariffs, one for most favoured nations and one general list. The lower schedule for most favoured nations would then apply to imports from all signatory nations which had imported from the world on an average for the preceding three years an amount equal to 90 per cent or greater of its total exports, on current account, averaged over the same three years. Nonsignatory nations would be subject to the general list.
The effect of this mechanism would be to provide each nation with a real and tangible incentive to buy from the world approximately the same value of goods and services it hoped to sell to the world. It would also alleviate, if not eliminate, present problems related to the convertibility of currencies. Customs regulations and other devices would not be able to frustrate the workings of international trade because each nation would be able to freely choose whether it wished its exports to receive most favoured nation treatment or not, and there would be a natural and automatic corrective.
Assuming, Mr. Speaker, that some such arrangement could be agreed upon, and that it did encourage world trade on an unprecedented scale, we still have another grave and urgent problem which faces us. It is the disparity of living standards between the peoples of our several countries. Particularly the gap in standards between Canada and the United States on the one hand, and various countries of Africa and Asia on the other hand is most striking.
One does not need to be a historian to know that many wars have been caused by political decisions taken on the basis of economic facts. Without going into a dissertation on the relative merits of the ascetic as against the opulent or abundant life, it suffices to say that from the beginning of time there has been conflict between the "haves" and "have nots". Here again there is both a moral and a practical aspect. There is no question morally but that we should help the people of the less developed nations to bring their standard of life more closely in equilibrium with our own. From the practical aspect, we have to do it or as surely as night follows day someone will ultimately wrest from us
492	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Hellyer our apparent material advantage. As so often is the case, the moral solution and the one which might be described as enlightened self-interest are identical. How then can we accomplish this goal in an orderly and acceptable manner?
Trade, not aid, is the cry. How often have we heard these words hollowly sung. And yet that simple idea states briefly and accurately the only workable solution. The less developed countries do not want largesse. It is suspect. It is also humiliating and takes away their self-respect. Proof of this lies in the fact that after our most generous neighbours, the people of the United States, have given tens of billions in aid to countries all over the globe that they are not really liked, collectively, in most of these nations. Aid smacks too much of the rich aunt or uncle patronizingly doling out various amounts in accordance with the likeability of the nephew or the relative merit of the project.
Please do not misunderstand me, Mr. Speaker. I do not mean that financial aid, technical assistance, etc., should be withdrawn. The point I am trying to make is simply that aid with or without strings attached is no solution. Trade, not aid, is the acceptable long term solution to equate the relative standards around the world. As I said earlier, it would be quite unrealistic and impractical for even the most fanatic free trader to suggest the removal of all trade barriers at this time. How then can we pay the idea more than lip service, without bringing about a chaotic result?
The answer, might be tied in directly with my earlier proposal for a new general agreement. Once the nations and peoples of the world accept the necessity of such a course of action, and are willing to go the second mile and make the proposal work, the action can be complementary and continuous.
I would suggest, therefore, that when the schedules of tariffs had been agreed upon by the signatory nations that they would then agree to reduce the most favoured nation schedule of tariffs by a minimum of one-fiftieth per annum and the general list by one-hundredth per annum. That means that at the end of 50 years all tariff barriers would be removed between trading nations. The general list reduced by half would still apply to nations which chose to restrict imports below the required level.
What a prospect, Mr. Speaker. The whole world as one market. The possibilities are staggering and unlimited. Only by some such positive approach can we hope to achieve a lasting peace in the world and good will between men; alleviate the unemployment at
IMr. Hellyer.]

home and raise the standard of life everywhere. The time has come when we must take our stand!

Mr. Speaker, it is not without some diffidence that the youngest member from Quebec is venturing upon his maiden speech in the House of Commons. To me, and to a great many of us, the first session was a period of adaptation after the result of the recent election.
Once we are more familiar with customs of parliamentary life, we find it easier to join the great family forming this house, and to bring our contribution, however small it might be.
It is with great pleasure that I associate myself with previous speakers in congratulating the members for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman), for Springfield (Mr. Slogan), for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin), for Trinity (Hon. Paul Hellyer), who, at the beginning of this new session, joined the parliamentary fraternity.
I congratulate the hon. member for Proven-cher (Mr. Jorgenson) and the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet who, as mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, brilliantly outlined various problems, the one about our greatest national asset, agriculture, and the other on national unity, a purpose that all here should strive to achieve.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words about the constituency of Beau-harnois-Salaberry, which I have the honour to represent in this parliament. On March 31, 1958, the people in my constituency celebrated a fiftieth anniversary. It had been 50 years since a Conservative member had represented that constituency in the parliament of Canada. To find the last Conservative member, defeated in 1908, we have to go away back to the time of Mr. J. H. G. Bergeron, nicknamed the "Beauharnois boy", who might be remembered by several of the senior members of this house.
The constituency of Beauharnois-Salaberry which extends from Chateauguay to the U.S. border, and through the cities of Beauharnois, Salaberry and Valleyfield, is comprised in a triangular area which, according to economists, is the Quebec area where the greatest development will occur in the next 20 years.
This year will be an historic one for Canada; it will mark the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway, and the beginning of a new era. The constituency of Beauharnois-

Salaberry right by the new seaway, should be the scene of a new development in various industrial fields, since on both sides of the canal which crosses my constituency for a distance of about 15 miles, there are vast parcels of land that would be ideal locations for new industries. We must not forget that today Beauharnois is synonymous with hydroelectric power. In fact, within the next few months, that plant will be able to supply over
2.200.000	horse-power. This power is bound to attract many industrialists looking for suitable locations for new plants to supplement the many others already established in the constituency.
I think it would be advisable to consider expanding the port facilities at Beauharnois, so as to relieve the congestion at Montreal harbour and to reduce shipping costs of plants already located in the area, such as the Aluminum Company of Canada, the Electro Metallurgical Company and the Standard Chemical Company, all of which are expanding their plants this year, which shows their confidence in the Canadian economy.
The constituency of Beauharnois, like the others, is faced with many more or less serious problems.
All levels of government should, therefore, try to have answers ready for future problems.
In my constituency as elsewhere, there is unemployment although, incidentally, it is now 15 to 20 per cent less than it was last year. I think it is high time our friends opposite stopped juggling with the figures, for they are distorting the picture and destroying people's confidence.
One of the main problems facing the citizens of Salaberry-de-Valley field, the largest city in my constituency, has to do with textile products.
The plant operated by Montreal Cottons Limited, largest plant of its type in the area, also the oldest since it dates back to 1873, has run into many problems in the past few years.
About eight years ago, this firm had some
3.000	people on its pay roll; right now it has about half that number, or just above 1,500.
A couple of years ago the firm spent some $5 million on plant modernization and expansion, and to iron out difficulties it had been experiencing for some years.
The Address-Mr. Bruchesi
Surely this should set a fine example for Canadian manufacturers and show them that even in a recession they should not be afraid to invest more capital, not only to increase production but especially to improve the quality of their products.
We have become accustomed to seeing delegations come to Ottawa for assistance from the central government. Personally, I feel that the government should give consideration to those who are trying to help themselves. The present plight of the textile industry is part of the legacy left to us by the Liberal party, a legacy we could have well done without but which the Conservative party accepts, to prove to the growing Canadian nation that the Liberal party is unworthy of the overrated reputation it has claimed credit for over the past 22 years.
The textile industry is the economic foundation of many communities in Canada. It is a noteworthy fact that textile imports account for 55 per cent of our total consumption. If only from 65 to 70 per cent of textiles consumed in Canada were of domestic manufacture, that industry could provide jobs for the 2,500 people, more or less, who are looking for work in the district of Valleyfield, and who would be very delighted to be able to work and to live normally, as it is their right, and consequently, to contribute to the economic growth of this nation.
The amounts made available to builders, by the government, through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, have enabled some 800 new families of the Chateau-guay area to move into a house of their own in 1958. Incidentally, this is hardly an indication of distress, as hon. members opposite would have us believe. Those developments are creating many problems in the various growing municipalities. It might therefore be advisable to renew the winter works offer, so that more municipalities can take advantage of this program next winter. This would also help in a tangible way to lessen the seasonal winter slump and consequently, to eliminate many of our governments' worries.
Being of the younger generation, and aware of the many problems facing the young people of Canada, I suggest that the government ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), to launch a campaign to advertise the benefits of greater specialization. A campaign such as I suggest would reduce the

The Address-Mr. G. R. Muir available labour force, would encourage more young men to learn a trade, would increase their productive capacity, would lower the production costs and, as a consequence, would enable manufacturers to get a larger share of world markets and to face the growing competition of many countries which, until now, had kept out of international trade.
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has won the esteem of the people of Canada, will do much to help us realize our dearest ambition, the happiness of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, on rising to make my contribution to this debate I first want to express my personal pleasure at your still occupying the very important position to which you were elected in 1957. In that position you have gained the respect and high regard of all hon. members. The gentleman to whom I am referring is not in his accustomed place at the moment but I hope he will receive this message.
At the same time, I would like to tell the Deputy Speaker and the deputy Chairman of the committees of the whole house that these expressions apply to them as well. At this time I should like also to offer my sincere congratulations to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
As has been indicated by previous speakers, it is the general opinion of this house that these two gentlemen made an excellent contribution to this debate.
Although I have had the privilege of speaking in this house on other occasions, this is the first time the opportunity has presented itself for me to take part in the debate on the throne speech. As a member from Manitoba representing the federal riding of Lisgar, I consider it my duty to endeavour to interpret the views of those whom I represent, and to place those views on the records of this house. This is particularly important since it is a well known axiom that as Manitoba goes, so goes the nation. The truth of this statement was borne out, I think, in the last general election.
At the outset, however, I should like to tell hon. members, with some pardonable pride, something about the people and the economy of my riding, the fertility of its soil, the well kept farms and the progressive
[Mr. Bruchesi.l

towns and villages within the area whose names are widely known throughout this country. One of the reasons for this, of course, is that the blood lines of our people stretch into every ethnic group and into almost every locality. The area was settled by the people from the counties of Ontario and Quebec in the 1870's. They were joined by members of different ethnic groups who, at that time, were helping to colonize our nation. I think the population of this riding today represents a real cross-section of the Canadian people. These descendants of the French, English, German, Irish, Icelandic, Scots, Scandinavian, Ukrainian, Dutch and Flemish settlers have learned to live and work together in a spirit of true Canadianism.
In my remarks about the riding, I should first mention that the eastern end of the riding is in the famous Red River valley, that flat, fertile bottom of a prehistoric lake called lake Agassiz. This particular area is one of the few remaining in Canada that has a soil and climate suitable for growing small fruits and vegetables, as well as various other crops, on a commercial basis. I would suggest that when the time has come when you have completely paved that fertile area in Ontario called the Niagara peninsula, you will have to depend on this particular area in Manitoba for your supply of fruits and vegetables. At the present time, the area is short of a water supply which would enable us to make full use of our potential production, and for processing and manufacturing purposes. I would commend to the government that serious consideration be given to joining with the government of Manitoba, under the terms of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, to provide the necessary funds for the construction of the capital works needed to provide water for the area.
The western end of the constituency encompasses one of the finest areas in western Canada for the production of livestock and grain, and is served by the excellent towns and villages located on the three provincial trunk highways running parallel throughout the length of the area. Within the constituency, stretching from the United States boundary north to the Assiniboine river, there has been developed a unique diversified type of agriculture. The production of alfalfa, registered seed, canning crops, poultry, livestock, and mink-ranching has helped stabilize the economy of the district. As a consequence related industries have also been developed. Canneries, creameries, hatcheries, plant nurseries, poultry and feed processing and seed cleaning plants are strategically placed amongst the progressive towns in the district.

We are fortunate also in having an outstanding experimental farm located near the town of Morden. This farm has helped immeasurably in the development of the area and has demonstrated the possibilities of varied production. With an assured water supply for our town and for agriculture this area could well become one of the most productive in the nation.
During this debate we have listened day after day to the purveyors of gloom on the other side of this house. I would suggest to those gentlemen that they should not confuse self-pity with concern for their fellow citizens. If they really want to be of service to the people of Canada, they should forget the last election and raise their eyes to the future. It has been said on many occasions by the leaders of both political parties that the last half of the twentieth century belongs to Canada. This, I believe, could come true, provided we grasp the opportunities afforded us in this bountiful land. However, the last half of the twentieth century is not going to be handed to us on a silver platter. In order to make sure it is going to be ours, we must do everything possible to earn it.
This fact imposes on us, as citizens and groups of citizens, certain obligations. We must be prepared to subvert selfish personal and regional interests to the national interest. The various groups within our economy, including labour and industry, must heed the advice of our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to hold the line on wages and profits in order that we do not price ourselves out of world markets and out of our home markets as well. There is also an obligation to produce at reasonable prices, to assist our primary producers who are doing their share to hold the price line in this country.
I was interested in hearing the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) give figures in his recent address showing that the cost-price squeeze on agriculture had lessened by some nine percentage points in 1958. I hope this trend continues until our farmers are on an equal footing with the other segments of our economy. As a farmer, I am concerned about any reversal of this trend which would result in a further reduction of farm income with its consequent adverse effects on the whole economy.
As a representative of an agricultural constituency I find that our farmers are appreciative of the fact that we now have a government which recognizes that our producers have been faced with problems beyond their own control. This government, recognizing those problems, took certain steps to correct the situation. No responsible person
The Address-Mr. G. R. Muir would suggest that the solution of these problems is easy or that they will be solved immediately. However, the government has charted a program aimed at providing for agriculture an economic climate in which our farmers will be able to better their own positions. It is a continuing process this session. Amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act should assist our farmers to improve their operations. The crop insurance program, carried out in co-operation with interested provincial governments-and the government of Manitoba is one of those-will be a real help in stabilizing farm income.
I believe the majority of western farmers have accepted the principle of the acreage payment as made by the government last year as the most equitable basis upon which supplementary payments can be made, since it recognizes each farmer and his family as being of equal importance to the nation. It compensates the small farmer for his higher costs of production and recognizes the need of the farmer who, through no fault of his own, either harvested a small crop or no crop at all. As a further example of the determination of this government to protect our farmers, the Prime Minister has stated that the Crowsnest pass rates on grain are regarded as a farmer's Magna Carta and as such must not be changed.
It is actions such as this that reassure our farmers with respect to the agricultural policies of this government and give us hope that those policies will attain for agriculture that measure of security and stability for which they are intended.
The prairie region usually has its quota of seasonal unemployed, particularly at this time of year, but figures released on January 16 of this year indicate that in that region applications for employment are down from the figure of a year ago. In Winnipeg, the largest centre of employment in Manitoba, the situation is particularly encouraging, with employment applications down by over 2,600 from the figure for the same date last year.
The fact that the home owner applicant is now able to apply directly to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for his loan should further encourage the home building program. This applies particularly to the smaller centres. With further funds to be made available by parliament this session-it was announced this morning that it would be an extra $250 million-this should prove to be a decisive factor in the employment situation for 1959.
I have some interesting figures on the total money spent in Manitoba on housing under the national housing scheme last year. The total amount of money spent on direct
496	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Gour loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and guaranteed loans under the National Housing Act amounted to $38,023,449. The number of loans was 2,887 and the number of units constructed was 3,800, which would make a sizable city. There is every reason to believe that this high level of construction will continue this year in view of the encouragement being received from this government.
As a Manitoban I was pleased with the announcement of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) that Winnipeg would be one of the stop-overs in the connecting link between the Atlantic and Pacific flights of the Canadian Pacific Air Lines. That city is destined to become a major airport in the future of air travel, lying as it does in the path of the transpolar flights. Anything that is done to speed that process is a source of satisfaction, of course, to all Manitoba members who have become more than ever convinced, as we face the future, that Manitoba is indeed the keystone province of our nation. If the axiom "as Manitoba goes, so goes the nation" applies economically as well as politically, the housing development and building program contemplated for that province this year, with its beneficial effect on its economy, should be reflected across this country; and we as Canadians can have every confidence in the continued development within our nation throughout 1959.

Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure indeed that I second the non-confidence motion proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), in which he clearly states that he has no confidence in the present government; and he is right. Poor Conservatives! Many of them are nice chaps, but they cannot make a go of running the affairs of this country! The situation today is no different from what it was between 1911 and 1921, and between 1930 and 1935. It has happened again in 1957 and will last until the people vote against the government at the next election.
Many of the Conservatives are clever, but they have no management ability, although, as regards their personal affairs, they are pretty good. I know that some of them are millionaires-and it is always among the Conservatives that we find the millionaires- but when it comes to managing the country's business, it seems they just can't do it. They manage to enact legislation that favours the rich and, needless to say, such legislation is hardly ever of benefit to the poor. I was very much amused this morning, listening to


the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) making his little political speech. However, it does not befit the head of so important a department to waste the few moments it took him to blame the official opposition, because the opposition has been telling the government some home truths, it has proved that the present administration is no good, and has said that the way the country is being run now will lead to the same situation as we have known under the Conservative regime during the terrible and dark years of 1930-35, as I explained when I addressed the house last Monday.
The Minister of Transport is a nice chap, very personable, tall and handsome, and flashes a pleasant smile; but he spent part of his time running down the official opposition, saying time and again that we, the Liberals, lacked confidence in our country. Now this is quite false. Under the Liberal administration we have proven beyond any doubt that we had faith in Canada and we still have that faith to-day. Instead of this the minister should have told the house, and Canadians, what he has in mind to improve the management of this country. He merely ranted at the official opposition, going over what the Liberals had done. And yet, we are telling our friends on the other side what they should be doing for the proper management of this country's affairs and keep it away from bankruptcy.
They have no right to tell us, Liberals, that we have no faith in our country. Instead of this they should change their behaviour here in the house. I don't mean they are doing it on purpose, but it seems to have grown into a habit with them, and they don't realize they are doing it.
We have faith in Canada. We have faith in the ability of all Canadians and in the future of Canada. This is something we have repeated time and time again and no one should be accusing us of the contrary. Canadians are not the only ones to have faith in their country; all nations in the world have faith in it too, and besides they had faith in the Liberal party and that is why thousands of individuals from every part of the world would have liked to emigrate to Canada. What is true, however, is that the people have no faith in the present government. Why? Because they remember what happened in the thirties. Besides at the time the Liberals were in office, thousands of people would have emigrated to Canada and settled here, if we had been able to let them in. But today these people no longer want to come because they have no confidence in the present government. We have proof of

this in the last two by-elections which took place in the riding of Trinity (Ontario) and in Springfield (Manitoba) where the Conservatives were reported to have done all they could to win those seats. They spared no effort to get those two seats; and yet, they were defeated in Trinity, and, had it not been for bad weather, even though they fought like mad, they would also have taken a licking in Springfield.
