You will see that next time it will be the same in Montmagny-L'Islet.
No, if we lack faith it is not a lack of faith in Canada, even though the minister kept repeating this throughout his speech, but a lack of faith or confidence in the Conservative government and in the way it is being managed.
Oh, you will say: "The people voted for us." Yes, they did for a time, because they accepted your promises, and I don't blame them. They thought you were sincere. But they have had their lesson and they realized what could happen. There are people in my constituency who shed tears every day because they believed in your promises. But make no mistake, the great majority of people in Canada are keenly disappointed, as evidenced by what I have just said. No, Mr. Speaker, no one will give credit to the statements of the Minister of Transport who, as I just pointed out, looks bright, seems fully qualified for the position he holds, but is, after all, only a plain small politician.
What the people of Canada want to know from the ministers and from the Conservative government, is what they intend to do to bring an end to unemployment, inflation and the present economic recession. That is what the people of Canada want to know from this government. Government members have been asking us to tell them how to run the country and when we do tell them how to go about it, they shoot back that we do nothing but criticize. After all, what else can we do but criticize them, and give them advice; we are not the ones who are running the country; if we were we would be running it the right way. Right now the Conservatives are entrusted with the affairs of Canada and it is not up to us to suggest this or that legislation, and every time there is a vote, they are extremely submissive. In fact, they listen to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) even more than a two-year old baby would listen to his mother. And because they are such obedient followers of the ministers, whenever there is a vote, we know ahead of time that we are defeated.
The Address-Mr. Gour
I shall be glad when the parliamentary secretaries are finally appointed, because then many Conservative members will be in a better position to quit their party when they realize that they were not among the elect. Then they will say: "I think I had better move in with the Grits and vote against the Tories", and by that time they will have good reasons to have confidence in the prosperity of their country.
As I said last Monday, under the Conservatives, from 1930 to 1935, the government was paying workers at Rockcliffe airport 2 cents an hour. As soon as the Liberals came back into power in 1935, wages immediately went up to 45 cents an hour, and these men were putting in an eight hour day. When we got out of office in 1957, tradesmen's wages in Canada averaged $1.25 to $3.00 an hour. That is what workers were being paid, according to the trade they practiced. We had brought back prosperity to the country. Yet, we had taken over a bankrupt government, and the war, which started in 1939, entailed tremendous expenditures. Our war effort which lasted almost 6 years, compared favourably with that of any other country which we went over to defend. In fact, if the population of Canada is compared with that of those other countries, it will be seen that we took better care of our servicemen than did any of those countries, and that better than any of them we helped our veterans and not only those of World War II but those of World War I, for the latter had a raw deal at the hands of the Conservative government, which had given them nothing on their return. In fact, with what they were getting, they had barely enough to buy a suit of clothes which at the time cost $75. Having only $10 left the returned men could not buy themselves shoes, socks or gloves. And that was all they got.
Furthermore, we helped them settle on farms and find jobs in industry. We also paid part of the tuition fees of those who sought higher education or wanted to take up a profession. We also helped those who wished to build themselves a house or start a small business, even a printing shop.
All this was making the country prosperous. Nearly all Canadian veterans were able to get jobs to provide their families with a decent living. In fact, between 1945 and 1957, there was prosperity in Canada such as no other country has ever enjoyed, a degree of prosperity unprecedented in the history of this country. And yet our hon. friends opposite dare ask: "What did you do in the 22 years you were in power?" My answer to this is: the Liberal party did

The Address-Mr. Gour so much for Canada that if a person went out to certain parts of the country which he had not visited for 5, 10 or 15 years, he would hardly know how to find his way in any village or small town and, of course, still less so in the larger cities. He would not be able to find his way, because of the changes wrought from one end of the country to the other.
The Liberal party can claim credit for the construction of over a million homes, and for the establishment of thousands of plants throughout the country. It looked after the development of our national resources, and provided Canadian citizens with the opportunity of proving their ability. Citizens rose to the challenge and made of Canada one of the most prosperous countries in the world, considering its limited population.
We started building the trans-Canada highway so that Canadians could travel from one end to the other of this beautiful country. We Liberals also drew up the plans of the St. Lawrence seaway, and almost completed this project to improve shipping conditions. We also built the pipeline which now enables us to carry to all other provinces, oil buried in the soil of Alberta, thereby providing jobs for thousands of Canadians.
We made huge sums available for the building of hospitals and universities. We introduced social legislation such as family allowances, veterans' assistance, old age assistance and unemployment insurance. We can also claim credit for drawing up all plans regarding health insurance.
Furthermore, we appointed a Canadian as Governor General. We abolished appeals to the privy council, making our supreme court the highest court in the country.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, we built a very substantial part of the trans-Canada highway, but we did not stop there. We introduced television and contributed to the progress of the National Research Council. We set up the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which, according to claims of our friends opposite, was set up only recently. Furthermore, we established fourteen crown companies. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal party's achievements are so numerous that I shall not take up more of the time of the house in enumerating them.
Mr. Speaker, I said a moment ago that the Liberal party had appointed a Canadian to the high position of Governor General. I take this opportunity of suggesting to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)-I see
that he has just gone out, but I am making the suggestion just the same-that it would be fitting, when the time comes to appoint a successor to the Governor General, when his term of office has expired, to follow a tradition that has been established in the House of Commons and in the Senate with regard to the choice of the Speaker, that is, that a French-speaking representative replaces an English-speaking representative and vice versa.
I hope that the new Governor General will again be a Canadian, for there are many Canadians who could very creditably fill this position. I do not see why one should oppose the selection of qualified men just because in the past they may have participated in the nation's political life. In support of my suggestion, I could mention the case of our judges who are always appointed by the party in power. Whether they have been in politics in the past or not, whether they are appointed by the provinces or by the federal government, these people cease to be in politics as soon as they are appointed, and I do not think I am mistaken in saying that we have the reputation of having judges who are as competent and, if I may say so, even much more competent, than those of any other country. We know that judges are very often selected among men of a recognized standing and who have played an active role in the political life of our country. Therefore, I do not see why our Governor General could not be a Canadian citizen; I would even prefer that he be selected among the Conservatives, if necessary, rather than have a representative from abroad.

Therefore the population of my constituency increased by 68,000, which means that since my friend's awakening, some 25,000 homes have been built in Russell constituency. Before my hon. friend's awakening, over 1 million new homes were built in Canada. He didn't know that, so I am telling him. And, at the time, it was much more difficult to build houses. When my good friend was sitting on this side of the house, he used to say: "Shortage of manpower"; you can't get either materials or labour. True, building materials were hard to get. And there was no unemployment. Today, 750,000 unemployed are looking for work and you can get all the materials you need, one hour after placing the order.
You should be in a position to build this year at least 200,000 new houses. The population of Canada is increasing at the rate of 400,000 each year. All you have to do is to get ready accordingly, and figure on the basis of three people per house. Therefore we will need over 135,000 to 140,000 houses a year. Besides there are many old houses that need to be repaired. With all this unemployment, and because of your lack of ability, the least you can do is to build houses.
You should build 200,000 houses this year. It is better to build houses, to do something worthwhile that will be an asset to the country. And it would be much more useful than to pay some $500,000,000 in unemployment insurance benefits, because it is better to give workers wages than to pay them $25 or $30 a week for doing nothing. If you pay them $50-$100 a week in wages for work done, at least we will have something left of this.
I want to make a suggestion that would promote construction. Indeed, many of you will say that it is incorrect, but I suggest that the interest rate on housing loans should not exceed 5 per cent.
Furthermore, the sale of building lots should be supervised. There is too much unfair advantage taken of the people in the


sale of land. The government should intervene. There is no reason why building lots should sell for $4,000, $5,000 and even $6,000. In fact, a man has to pay $25 a month for 25 years to pay principal and interest on the lot. The government, with the co-operation of the provinces, should contribute to the cost of sewer and water systems in new districts. This would reduce the cost of housing and would further encourage Canadians to become house owners.
Mr. Speaker, our good friends opposite should manage the business of the country in the proper way. At the time of the Liberals, we used to sell aircraft to our good neighbours, and to other countries. According to newspaper reports, the government is disorganizing our aircraft factories. Yet this industry is very important for the defence of our country and for our civil aviation.
Our engineers and specialists are going to the United States. Consequently, our workers stay here without work.
During the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958, it was said that we were buying too much from our good friends to the south, that we should divert 15 per cent of our purchases to commonwealth countries. Naturally, this was intended to win the election. But today, when we are buying Bomarcs, aircraft, etc., from the United States, we are making Canada dependent on the United States for our defence.
That is the way the Conservatives understand politics. The hon. member who spoke before me referred to the good job that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) has done for the country. I didn't say that you are all bad boys, because many of you are good boys; the only trouble with you is that you are Conservatives, and that, as such, you do not know how to run the country.
I think I know my way in the field of agriculture. The market price of butter was 64 cents; you lowered it to 63 cents. Powdered milk was 17 cents, I believe, and you cut down the price by 3 cents, so that it would not look too bad. But things are bad, and could be even worse. Do you know why they are not worse? It is no fault of yours, nor is it the Liberals' fault! It is because the Americans are buying our cattle. However, I want to tell you now that if the Americans are buying our cattle, it is because of an agreement entered into by the Liberals with the U.S.A. If Americans should stop buying our cattle, I do not think that the Conservative government could come to a new agreement with them. I recognize, however, that you have provided a substantial aid to western farmers; it is an average of $200 for each farmer, whether or not he was a millionaire. But that is not the way to run this country!
Mr. Speaker, my remarks are sincere and I hope that they will be received as constructive criticism, for the welfare of Canada. I cannot get used to the idea that after four years of bad Conservative administration, and in spite of my age, I will not see another era of prosperity.

The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet made a speech in this house, which I think was a tremendous contribution to this debate,
The Address-Mr. McGrath when he spoke on a subject which we in eastern Canada-and I mean eastern Canada-are so deeply interested in, namely national unity. I would compliment the hon. member, but at the same time ask him and other hon. members to bear in mind, in developing this theme of national unity, that we in Canada should develop a national unity without uniformity. Canada is developing into a great nation comprised of many races, people of many ethnic origins, and to my mind each has something to contribute more fully to a greater Canada by retaining those traditions, those colourful traditions of his national origin, traditions, which I suggest are contributing to make a new and more distinctive kind of Canadian.
This year will mark the tenth anniversary of the entry of my province into this family of Canadian provinces. I like to think- and perhaps this thought is shared by other hon. members-that perhaps one of the greatest contributions my province made to the Canadian family was to contribute to the Canadian scene a culture and a tradition which are rooted in folklore, a folklore in the traditions of Devon, of the west country, of Scotland and of Ireland, folklore and traditions which have been carefully retained and protected down through the years.
As a member from the most easterly constituency in Canada, Mr. Speaker, I was interested to notice in the speech from the throne a reference to freight rates. The quotation reads:
My ministers will recommend to you action to alleviate the discriminatory effects of the recent horizontal increase in freight rates.
I cannot tell you how keenly we look forward to this measure being introduced because we are at the extreme eastern end of the line. We are at the mercy of the railways and the future of what secondary industry we have in my city and my constituency solely depends on such a measure.
While on the subject of transportation, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read into the record a statement of the president of the Canadian National Railways, which he made in Halifax on November 20 or 21, 1958. It is taken from the St. John's News and is a Canadian Press dispatch. Mr. Gordon said:
Sensational reports about the Canadian National Railways ferry, William Carson, having trouble docking at Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, are doing a disservice to the maritimes and alarming the tourist trade.

The Address-Mr. McGrath
The statement goes on:
I am surprised that the newspapers of this area make so much of the fact that wind blows in this part of the world and interferes with shipping.
In addition to that statement for the record, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give you briefly the record of the service of the William Carson and which I might add bears the name of a distinguished Newfoundlander, Dr. William Carson, who carried on the fight for responsible government in Newfoundland more than a hundred years ago. The figures that I have cover the period from October 6, 1958 to December 31, 1958. During 13 trips of the William Carson, which is our main link with the Canadian mainland, from North Sydney to Port aux Basques this ship which has been surrounded with so much misfortune was delayed for a total period of 237 hours and 20 minutes; 237 hours and 20 minutes lost in 13 trips. I have more comprehensive figures, but I will not detain the house with them at this time. However, I do propose to go into this more fully during the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees). The point I would like to make is this:	I respectfully suggest that the Department of Transport take steps to place the William Carson in a service where she can do the most good. The Newfoundland board of trade has offered the suggestion that the William Carson should operate from North Sydney to Argentia, of which I am sure the minister is most familiar. I would like to state for the record that I feel such a service is the only justification we have for, and it is the only way that we can fully take advantage of such a modern and beautiful ship.
Not only that but I would like to bring home the fact that in my province, with which I realize perhaps most Canadians are not too familiar, we are two separate regions. We have no transinsular highway; hence we have only the Canadian National Railways which operate a single narrow gauge antiquated railway which was taken over from the Newfoundland government in 1949. Consequently the people of the west coast of Newfoundland and of the east coast have little or no communication with each other. It is with this point in mind that I would support the claims of the Newfoundland board of trade and respectfully suggest that the passenger ferry, William Carson, which carries the name of such a noted Newfound-

lander, in this tenth year of confederation be used to link the vast population of this country who are living on the east coast of Newfoundland with the mainland.

speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was making reference to the record of the Canadian National Railways' ferry William Carson, which operates from North Sydney to Port aux Basques, the western terminus of the Newfoundland service of Canadian National Railways. Time will not permit me to delve further into this contentious subject. For the time being, I shall let the record speak for itself.
During this debate we have heard continuous remarks from hon. gentlemen opposite to the effect that this government has done nothing to relieve the unemployment situation in Canada. I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite must have read and listened to the speech from the throne, as I have. I noticed several references in there. For example, there is a suggestion of the introduction of a measure to increase the funds under the National Housing Act from the consolidated revenue fund, boosting that fund to a billion dollars. Surely, this will have the effect of stimulating house construction in Canada, and it will have the related effect of providing jobs for Canadians from coast to coast. I do not believe it is necessary to go into the chain reaction that results from the building of a home.
There is a suggestion also in the speech from the throne concerning an increase in the total funds that may be expended under the Trans-Canada Highway Act. There is a reference to certain amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. In my own province of Newfoundland, the government has embarked on a program to relieve distress in the fisheries of Newfoundland by means of a program for the building of community stages. This initial program will cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $500,000 and there is some suggestion that the program will be carried out during the coming year. For the benefit of hon. gentlemen who perhaps do not know what a

community stage is, I would say that a community stage may be described as a central fish landing and processing building where the fishermen can prepare their fish for salting; salt, store and process the article under efficient, sanitary conditions. The stages will be managed and operated by a local authority or a fisherman's co-operative. The fishermen may continue to operate as individuals or pool their operations, as I mentioned, in a community enterprise.
This program is a joint undertaking by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean). I would suggest it is a step in the right direction. It is, perhaps, somewhat unfortunate that that program is not on schedule because of the severe winter conditions being experienced in my province of Newfoundland. The program will have the effect of providing direct employment for the hard-pressed fishermen of my province, another step in the right direction towards relieving the unemployment problem.
I would suggest that hon. gentlemen opposite should be constructive in their criticism instead of trying to propagate their fallacious doctrine of gloom and doom. In the limited time at any disposal, I should like to close by commenting on a suggestion which is, to me as a young Canadian an exciting one, and which will have an appeal, I feel, to all Canadians. This is a project national in scope and national in its significance.
I am sure all hon. members of this house have heard references to the establishment of a free port or a transshipment port on Canada's eastern seaboard, or more specifically on the island of Newfoundland. Such a port, located on our east coast would, in effect, receive the grain from the port of Churchill on Hudson bay and from the lakehead down to the St. Lawrence seaway, and there await transshipment in the grain elevators of this port to the markets of the world. This would, of necessity, have to be a deep water harbour, an ice-free harbour; it would, of necessity, have to be strategically located near what is known as the great circle shipping routes. In other words, it would have to be accessible to the trade routes of the world. We have two such harbours in the province of Newfoundland and, I might add, they are both located in the constituency of my friend the hon.
The Address-Mr. McGrath member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter). One is a great natural fiord on the southeast coast of Newfoundland called Head Bay d'Espoir. The other one, which is most often mentioned, is a beautiful natural inlet, the water-way of Mortier bay on the Burin peninsula.
In order to give you an idea of the strategic location of this great natural harbour I am sure you will be interested to learn that it is 700 miles closer to Gibraltar than is the port of New York. It is closer to the main ports of South America, Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Aires, than any single port in North America. These are interesting statistics. Furthermore, all the important trade routes originating from the English channel and the main industrial ports of Europe and which terminate in the western hemisphere pass within less than 100 miles of this great natural harbour on the east coast of Newfoundland. Such a transshipment port would be of immense value to the grain growers of Canada for it would result in reduced transportation costs. The advantages of such a development to my province cannot really be over-emphasized at this time. It would, in effect, mean the creation of a virtually new industry, a thriving industry, which would have a great effect on the economy of the Atlantic provinces.
There is now being shipped from the port of Churchill on Hudson bay something like 16 million bushels of wheat each year in a relatively short shipping season. The transportation of this grain requires somewhere in the vicinity of 50 ships. However, this is a somewhat costly means of transportation because these bottoms must arrive at the port of Churchill empty, with the resultant high cost of transportation. However, in spite of this fact, the use of this route results in substantial savings per bushel on the grain. If such a transshipment port were to be established, and if grain elevators were to be built on Canada's eastern seaboard, it is suggested that it would be possible to make a saving of four cents per bushel. I understand this would be a substantial saving indeed. This project can be projected as the ultimate expansion or the ultimate completion of the St. Lawrence seaway because in reality they virtually complement each other. Reference has been made to such a port by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo on another occasion and I would presume that it would receive the full support of the hon. gentleman.

The Address-Mr. Garland
The shores of Mortier bay, as most hon. gentlemen from my province will readily tell you, lend themselves by virtue of their terrain to the building of wharves, shipping docks, grain elevators, immense warehouses, factories and even a great new city. This might sound like an ambitious scheme, but all great schemes are founded on ambition. As I stated before, the economic advantages of such a national development to the economy of the Atlantic provinces and of Canada as a whole cannot at this time be fully appreciated. I would urge the members of the government and all hon. members of this house to acquaint themselves fully with the advantages, the possibilities and the potential of such a great national development.
May I close on the theme with which I started. The hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Fortin) eloquently expressed his theme of national unity. I would suggest that this would be a step in the direction of that greater national unity because it would have the effect of making the eastern seaboard, the Atlantic region of Canada, a more integral part of the economy of this nation. I feel it will warrant the serious consideration of this government, a government that has done more to develop this theme of national unity than has any other government since the days of Sir John A. Macdonald.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As usual, this task was carried out in a most commendable manner, bringing credit to both the mover and the seconder and to the ridings which they represent.
I should like to explain, Mr. Speaker, that I had not intended taking part in this throne speech debate because it semed to me that our leader made a brilliant, comprehensive review of the present situation, pointing out the many shortcomings of the government especially in respect of the lack of a clear-cut government policy. However, the contributions of the cabinet ministers in this debate have been so partisan and so void of policy that perhaps a word is necesary to remind them again that they are no longer in the opposition but that, as members of the government, they are expected to be providing leadership. Instead, they seem to be following a policy of opposition to the opposition.

The best example to illustrate my point was the political speech made in this debate by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) who devoted one part of his remarks to apologizing for his somewhat less than brilliant showing on "Press Conference" and the balance of his speech to criticism and belittling of Liberals, past and present. It was hardly the kind of speech expected in these critical times from one aspiring to be Minister of Trade and Commerce and hardly the kind of speech that would inspire much confidence throughout this country. I would ask businessmen looking for economic guidance with respect to the future to read that speech and judge for themselves.
This morning we had another rather strange utterance, this time from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) who should be in possession of the facts and who was again attacking the opposition concerning the use of statistics. I should like to refer to some figures the minister used. Pie made the extraordinary statement this morning that the Canadian merchant marine at the end of world war II consisted of 500 ocean-going ships. I am not going to pursue this point and I want to be fair to the minister. I know that he realizes that the statement he made was a grossly exaggerated one. The figure was not 500 but, to the best of my knowledge, was 173, practically all of which were built during the war for wartime use and were disposed of after the war.
Mr. Speaker, we have been listening for nearly ten days for something constructive from the government but what have we heard? We have heard from the government only criticism and further attempts to belittle our leader and to drag him down from the high place he so rightly occupies in the minds of people at home and abroad. Then there is this further and unfounded accusation by the government that we lack confidence in the economy. The only thing in this regard that the Liberal opposition lacks confidence in is the ability of the government to do its job. After all, it has been Liberal administrations that helped create the kind of economic climates in which Canada made its greatest progress over the years.
Then there is this further untrue accusation by the Conservatives, and they do it at every opportunity, that the Liberals did nothing for the commonwealth. This afternoon the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. JANUARY 29, 1959
Walker) read and referred to some newspaper clippings having to do with the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker's) recent commonwealth tour. But he apparently did not go far enough with his reading of those press clippings or he would have found some others. This came out at the time our present Prime Minister was visiting India; the story came out at that time, I believe. At the commonwealth conference of prime ministers in 1949 a Canadian formula was put forward by the Canadian government which made it possible for India to remain as a republic within the commonwealth.
Rarely, except in wartime, I suggest, has Canada's parliament met in a more difficult period. As has been pointed out, the two most difficult and most urgent problems are unemployment and inflation or, if you prefer, jobs and rising prices. However, there are many other serious problems confronting the Conservative administration as this new session gets under way. Canadians are facing the prospect of a billion dollar deficit as compared with regular reductions in our national debt from surpluses under Liberal administration. After many years of steady growth under Liberal administration, Canadians are witnessing our second year of slowdown in our national production. Indecision and uncertainty are dimming the 1959 prospects for the Canadian oil and natural gas industry. Canadians are concerned about the muddle in our defence policies and the lack of decision about building the Arrow fighter plane. Canadians are also concerned about our role in continental defence. I do not think anyone but the most partisan Tory would argue that Canada's role in international affairs has taken on added vigour under Conservative administration. I think it is fair to say that Canada's influence at the United Nations and at NATO has not been increased under the present government. Shrinking immigration with 125,000 immigrants last year as compared with 282,000 in 1957, with our economy under Conservative administration unable apparently to absorb more, according to government spokesmen, is a matter of real concern.
Another serious problem is the apparent lack of confidence resulting in the weakening of prices of Canadian bonds. This poses another real problem in the government's future financing.
Some of us have wondered why, in view of the importance of Canada-United States re-
The Address-Mr. Garland lations, the important position of ambassador to the United States was left unfilled for such a long period. However, we are all pleased to see that the matter has been corrected and we would hope not at the expense of the civil service commission.
In view of the ministers' partisan speeches I am tempted to bring up several shortcomings of the present government but I realize I must be careful lest we be named as one of Khrushchev's helpers. This seems to be the attitude of the present government toward any criticism. I suppose the pattern for this was set on the opening day of the debate by the Prime Minister in replying to my leader and is understandably repeated by aspiring government supporters. It seems rather strange that this new government, in power for such a relatively short time and so flush with criticism when in opposition, should be so sensitive about any criticism of their lack of policy.
Having due regard for the many factors contributing to our economic slow-down, I believe that a major factor was the shock of realizing on June 11, 1957 that Canada had lost its experienced government. This lack of confidence that became apparent so soon was not because it was a Conservative government but rather because it was an inexperienced government. Never since June, 1957 has it been so apparent that this new, inexperienced government is incapable of dealing with the problems of the day. I believe this lack of confidence has contributed substantially to the decline in capital investment by business, which has been one of the major contributing factors in our economic slowdown. This lack of confidence in the government is, I believe, more than justified. When we look around us today and see the mounting list of problems piling up over the last 18 months, it is little wonder that businessmen, both at home and abroad, are temporarily at least delaying many of their expansion plans and taking a second look.
What a difference a year makes! What a difference between Canada under Liberal administration in 1956 and under Conservative administration in 1958. During the 10 years previous to the Conservatives coming into office the Liberal administration was able to reduce taxes by substantial amounts every year except in the year of the Korean incident. In addition to these substantial tax reductions, the Liberal administration was able to effect substantial reductions in our national debt. These reductions in our national debt during the last 10 years have

The Address-Mr. Garland been wiped out in the last 18 months by Conservative patchwork policies.
Yes, indeed, what a difference a year makes! Canadians were shocked to find that between Harris in 1957 and Fleming in 1958 there was a difference of $1,200 million. That is what it cost the Canadian people to change their administration from Liberal to Conservative. This new Conservative government may well go down in history as the most expensive luxury Canadians ever had. It is little wonder that investors are concerned about the new government.
I should like to say a word about the problem of steadily rising unemployment. The only words of encouragement that the government seems to have offered over the past few months are utterances from time to time that the unemployment situation is worsening at a slower rate than before. This is not much comfort to the person who is without a job. The most recent figures show that one worker in every fifteen is without work, with every indication that the situation will be worse. I say it is a disgrace that in this young, vigorous and rich country we must accept the proposition from our government that two millions of our men, women and children must suffer as a result of unemployment this winter. The average Canadian is understandably shocked by the situation. Despite the fact that hundreds of millions have been poured into our economy, with a maximum of publicity by the government, we find more people seeking jobs since the Conservatives took over than at any time since the depression of the thirties when they were last in office.
The government cannot shirk its responsibility. Surely the government's failure to deal adequately with unemployment is well recognized. Even today they apparently are not ready with any legislation to ease unemployment this winter or they would have taken advantage of our proposal to terminate the throne speech debate. Surely it is the responsibility of the federal government to maintain a high level of employment. Surely they must now realize that relief measures, though helpful, are not a cure for unemployment.
In addition, we have the Prime Minister's own words that no person would be permitted to suffer from unemployment. Despite the fact that the number of unemployed is steadily rising, the government is almost daily taking credit for relieving the situation. They take special credit for their winter works program which provides for paying 50 per cent of the labour costs on projects that would not normally have been undertaken this winter. On the surface this looks like a sound proposal.


However, its soundness will be established only if it proves to be effective. To date, in the municipalities I have checked personally, I find it has been of little or no value.
After all, the labour costs on many municipal projects represent only a small portion of the over-all costs. This means that the municipalities in most cases, in order to take advantage of this offer, would have to assume substantial financial obligations to cover these capital outlays. These additional financial obligations have been made more costly by the government's actions in raising interest rates. The government's ill-fated conversion scheme, referred to by some as "Fleming's folly", which had the effect of increasing interest rates by 50 per cent on a substantial portion of government borrowing, has naturally had the effect of making provincial and municipal borrowing more expensive. In this field of government endeavour alone I think the government should be severely criticized. By increasing the cost of borrowing at the provincial and municipal levels the federal government has retarded, rather than encouraged, badly needed projects, projects that would have yielded much needed jobs not only on the projects themselves but in the production and transportation of the materials used.
As I indicated at the beginning, I do not intend to belabour the shortcomings of the government. These are well known. I simply wish to point out in a friendly way that the brave new world promised by the Conservatives prior to June, 1957 has failed to materialize.
It would seem that Conservative government policy falls into two broad categories: first, an attempt to outbid the Liberals with the people's own money and, second, that political expediency replace prudent planning. How often do we hear the expression that members of the government are acting like kids in toyland for the first time, trying out all the gadgets and free rides. I suggest that their journey into fairyland is over. Canadians expect them to stop acting and to settle down and grapple with these serious Canadian problems. Much valuable time has been lost already. This year Canadians will be expecting more on budget night than a blue message read from a blue lectern by a blue minister with a blue flower in his blue lapel.

I should like to turn now to problems directly affecting the district of Nipissing. Some few weeks ago Premier Frost

announced his government's intention to establish a port at Moosonee which would provide safe, all-year-round anchorage for ocean-going ships. At that time the premier said that the ocean port would be established with or without federal assistance. I realize that this is an election year in the province of Ontario and critics of the government may well be suspicious that this is an election promise. However, it seems that the Ontario government has approved $5 million to start the project and it is reported that engineers and drillers are currently on the site.
I know this matter has been discussed with the federal government and hope has been expressed that they will be sufficiently interested in the Moosonee project to build suitable docks there. It is also to be expected that private mining companies and others will be building their own docks. In addition, it is hoped that an all-weather landing strip will be constructed with the materials dredged from the bottom of the river. I should like to urge the cabinet to give this project its wholehearted support.
The establishment of this deep water port at Moosonee will make our whole northland readily accessible to the industrial centres of Canada. Here, it seems to me, is a readymade project which the federal government could readily endorse. This is a project that could be proceeded with now, not at some future imaginary date. I suggest this government, which has, by its statements, indicated such profound interest in northern development, do everything within its power to encourage its friends in Ontario to get on with this development. In this way they can silence the critics who would say that Ontario is only dragging this out because it is an election year. I urge the government to recognize that here is an opportunity to do one important but not costly thing for the 18 million Canadians we have today, rather than sit around dreaming about the 100 million of which the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) spoke on Monday.
I should also like to make a request of a regional nature concerning work on this Moosonee project. If the federal government does enter into an agreement with Ontario I would hope that since this is a northern Ontario project northern Ontario firms might be given every opportunity to participate in this development. I understand that contracts being carried out at the present time in connection with the preliminary surveys were awarded without asking northern Ontario firms to bid. On a local basis I can think of at least three or four drilling firms in my own city which are highly competent to undertake
The Address-Mr. Garland this work and which would have been most anxious to tender had they been given an opportunity.
In this connection I should like to suggest that when defence installations are made- I am referring now to the Bomarc anti-aircraft missile base-northern Ontario firms should be given every opportunity to participate. I recognize that these projects are of a national character and that discrimination cannot be shown against any firm, regardless of its location in Canada. However, I do urge that wherever possible local northern Ontario firms be given every opportunity to provide their services, having regard to their technical capabilities.
May I turn now to a matter of local and national interest, namely the plight of a basic Canadian industry, the manufacture of Canadian plywood. The plywood industry in Canada is divided into two main sections; softwood, which is for the most part Douglas fir produced in British Columbia and hardwood, produced in eastern Canada, the prairie provinces and British Columbia.
May I go a step further and explain that I am concerned primarily with one division of the hardwood plywood section which has to do with decorative hardwood plywood. The production of decorative hardwood plywood is centred in eastern Canada. It involves approximately 30 companies located in small communities in Ontario and Quebec. This industry employs about 4,600 persons, with an annual payroll of approximately $12 million and a production value of approximately $43 million. This industry is experiencing considerable difficulty and is currently operating at a depressed level. I am advised that in 1957 eight companies had a consolidated loss of approximately $575,000 as compared with an average profit of $1,316,000 during the four previous years.
The reason for this depressed state of the industry is well known to the government and especially to the members of parliament on both sides of the house who represent the constituencies where these plywood mills are located. It is reported that Japanese imports have actually captured more than 50 per cent of the hardwood plywood consumer market in Canada. This problem has resulted from the fact that Japanese plywood can be retailed in Canada for less money than it costs a Canadian manufacturer to produce. In January, a year ago, representatives of the industry discussed this matter with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and presented the problem squarely to him.

At that time the minister seemed interested in the problem and agreed to discuss the difficulty with the Japanese ambassador to see if some solution could not be worked out.
It is reported the minister found the Japanese government willing to apply voluntary controls on their plywood exports. A quota was to be placed on Japanese exports of plywood from April 1 to December 31 of last year. The Japanese plywood industry agreed to reduce its exports by 10 per cent from the 1957 levels. Figures for 1958, however, show that Japanese plywood exports to this continent are on the increase. Another highly important aspect of this situation is that shipment of veneers ready to be glued into plywood is in a category which falls outside the quota system. I recognize at once that there is no easy solution to this problem. However, the government must take action in the very near future if our Canadian hardwood plywood industry is to continue to exist.
Let me relate this problem to the local level. I have in mind the Guelph Plywood Company Limited with mills located at Mat-tawa, in the east end of the district of Nip-issing, and in Scotstown, Quebec-I hope the hon. member for that district will not object to my referring to his area. After 50 years of operation the plywood mill at Scotstown had to be closed, which removed from that community, I am told, virtually its sole means of support.
At Mattawa, a town of 3,500 people, the Guelph Plywood Company Limited is also the main source of employment. Since Japanese manufacturers have taken over 50 per cent of the North American plywood market the industry at Mattawa is considered to be in a dangerous position. Representations have been made to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) with regard to this danger and,

as I have mentioned, additional representations have been made to the government through the Minister of Finance.
The Guelph Plywood Company Limited have made every effort to sustain activity at Mattawa and have succeeded by the questionable means of exporting veneer to the United States instead of finished plywood. This is a retrograde step so far as Canada is concerned, inasmuch as it is using our nat-tural resources to our minimum advantage.
It should also be pointed out that while endeavouring to maintain activity at Mattawa the company has responsibilities to the provincial department of lands and forests for the upkeep of their licences in respect of the crown lands they hold. This company accepts and discharges these responsibilities at considerable cost. Means of recovering the outlays and promoting better forestry are greatly curtailed by the loss of markets. The Guelph Plywood Company's over-all employment payroll has fallen from approximately 300 people to less than half that figure. Their woods operations have been greatly curtailed with a production of logs of possibly half what it was previously.
This firm, as well as many others in the decorative hardwood plywood industry, are anxious to take their place as a sound Canadian industry, paying adequate wages, pursuing the best forestry practices, producing a volume of exports for the national benefit, and maintaining research facilities which will keep their industry to the forefront. This they cannot do under the circumstances in which they find themselves today.

This was moved by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on February 11, 1957, and had been moved before that and it was moved on other subsequent occasions:
This house is of the opinion that the welfare of the Canadian people requires the adoption now of a national development policy which will develop our natural resources for the maximum benefit of all parts of Canada, encourage more processing of those resources in Canada, correct the present serious unfavourable trade balances, foster wider

financial participation by Canadians in the development of our resources and promote greater opportunity and employment for a steadily increasing population.
Summed up, this means nation building, and tonight I propose to point out how we have been following this course since taking over the government of the country in 1957. I cannot deal with all of the questions which could be classified under this proposal but I shall deal with some. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, behind this policy is the belief that our nation, with its resources, not only raw materials but also lavish energy sources such as coal, oil and gas, hydroelectric power and uranium, and above all, with the courage, common sense and character of the Canadian people, can become one of the great nations of the world.
Let me tell the story briefly of our experience with housing, which is one way of building a nation and a very good way at that. I have here a clipping from the Vancouver Province of February 1, 1957. This was about four months before the defeat of the last government. The heading is:

The results, Mr. Speaker, as everyone will admit have been spectacular. In the last calendar year there were over 163,000 housing starts. We do not have the exact figures yet; it will be some days before we can give it exactly but this is about 25,000 units higher than the record in 1955 and it is over 40,000 higher than the number of starts in the calendar year 1957.
In so far as completions in 1958 are concerned, they have set a record of about 146,000 units. The previous record was 135,700 in the year 1956. The carry-over of houses under construction in Canada in midwinter is higher than it has ever been, about 88,000 units. Even more remarkable is the fact that there continues to be an excellent market for these homes. We have always watched very carefully for any indication that there were too many of these small homes being built. However, as of the end of December, there were only 3,239 which had been completed and were unoccupied, and that included single units and duplexes, whereas in December, 1957, there were 2,765. When you realize the greatly increased number of completions in 1958, you will see that there is, as yet, no indication that the market is breaking.
The officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have recently interviewed the heads of all the banks and lending institutions, and have been told that there will be about the same amount of money put up by these companies for mortgage lending in 1959. All indications are that this present year, 1959, will be another splendid year for house-building in Canada.
We believe that in our housing policy we are really building Canada. I have here a letter from the secretary-manager of the national retail lumbermen's council of Canada, dated November 26, in which he says:
I have been asked by the National Retail Lumbermen's Council of Canada to write to you and to express the sincere appreciation of the 2,000 lumber retail firms which make up its membership, for the forward thinking which has been exhibited by the federal government in making available the very large sums of money to assist in the housing program.
The members of the National Retail Lumbermen's Council of Canada are well aware of the very material benefits which have resulted from this action and feel that it has been most timely and beneficial to all segments of the Canadian economy as well as to their own businesses.

The Address-Mr. Green
We have had similar word from many other responsible organizations across the country. I do not believe anybody, even on the other side of the house, questions the accuracy of the statements contained in that letter.
So much for housing; then, I should like to tell briefly the story of the activities of the Department of Public Works in building Canada during the last year and in 1959. It should be realized that this is only one of the building departments. Transport, we think, gets more money than we do. Defence production and other departments also do building; in public works there has been a tremendous program under way from coast to coast. My officials tell me that there have been 292 different projects, all of them over $15,000, which would not ordinarily have been proceeded with in the fiscal year 1958-59. In addition to that, there have been many, many projects under $15,000.
I must admit it is a bit discouraging to a minister of public works to have lock-outs and strikes such as there were in Vancouver for the whole of this last summer when there were many millions of dollars worth of construction under contract and waiting to be done. This is one of the discouraging aspects, and I think it is an aspect which everyone, no matter what his political belief, should face.
Then, during the present winter, in addition to these programs I have mentioned we have had the winter work program in co-operation with the municipalities. The idea for this came from a very worth-while, informal conference between the members of the cabinet and the representatives of the various municipalities of Canada. Most of the outstanding mayors of the country came here last fall and gave us excellent ideas. One of them was this winter works program.
This program is so designed that it is available to every municipality. In fact, the first municipality in British Columbia to pay money under it was one of the very smallest, the municipality of Kent. This program is available to all the municipalities in Canada who wish to take advantage of it. There has been co-operation as well by the provincial governments. This has been a truly national co-operative effort, and I believe it is one which might very well be carried on every winter.
Then we have had a program of building small post offices across Canada. There have been between 65 and 70 small post offices rushed on in order to provide employment. There have been the community stages described this evening by the hon. member for

St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). These have all been worth-while projects, and certainly they have all helped. We do not have to offer any apologies for any of these programs. It is significant that general construction, including housing of course, was at a record level during the year 1958. The president of the Canadian construction association predicts that 1959 will see an even higher record.
Then I should like to go on for a few minutes to the broader aspects of national development policy. Here, too, we have a good story to tell. Let us consider the dam on the South Saskatchewan river. This project is actually under way. Contracts have been let. My, how long we would have had to wait for a Liberal government to get around to doing that particular one. This is a great nation-building project.
Then, there is the Columbia river. Here is another huge nation-building project. This afternoon you heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) read an announcement to the effect that the United States has now agreed that the question of downstream benefits should be worked out between the two sections of the international joint commission. This is the first time they have admitted that Canada is entitled to any downstream benefits. Here is a self-liquidating development which we believe can now go ahead with great benefit to both Canada and the United States and, above all, of great benefit to the people of my native province of British Columbia. If this project can be undertaken, it will mean great industrial development in the southeastern interior of British Columbia, in the Kootenay valley and in the Okanagan valley. It will mean cheap electric power in the lower mainland. It will give that province the greatest impetus it has ever had since its establishment over 100 years ago.
It is true that this project will depend upon the co-operation of the government of the province of British Columbia. They have been giving some indication that they would prefer to have a pet scheme of their own up on the Peace river developed by the Wenner-Gren interests. I can only say this. If this Columbia river project is killed by failure of the government of British Columbia to co-operate they will be doing a great disservice to the people of our province and to the people of Canada.
I wish to refer also to these famous old cities of Fort William and Port Arthur at the Canadian lakehead. They are greatly worried at this time. They see the St. Lawrence seaway being developed and they read in the Duluth News-Tribune of January 11

that a group of Canadians, if you please from Winnipeg are proposing to build a big port development at Duluth, Minnesota, for this purpose, and I quote from this article:
Freeman-
Mr. Freeman is the Winnipeg promoter of this scheme.
-is reported to have in mind making Duluth the port for the rapidly developing western Canadian provinces as well as the mid western and western parts of the United States.
This government has been greatly interested in the lakehead. For over a year we have had our engineers considering where best harbour terminal facilities could be installed. Then we engaged engineering consultants, Sir Alexander Gibb and Associates. They have just finished their preliminary report. There is some controversy as to which of two sites should be chosen. One of them is right at the boundary between the two cities. The other is over on the west side of Fort William. They have recommended that the site at the boundary should be used for these terminal facilities. The government intends to accept this recommendation and to get ahead with the construction of these harbour terminal facilities just as quickly as possible. The new harbour terminal will include the facilities for handling ocean-going ships and will assist the lakehead ports in meeting the changes in transportation patterns resulting from the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. The first tenders are expected to be called in the next two or three months. The preliminary estimate of the total cost of the development is approximately $5 million.
Then the lakehead has also been worried because of the threat of the closure of the Canadian car company's plant there. A few weeks ago members of the cabinet met a delegation from the lakehead, including the members; the mayors of the two cities; the provincial minister, Hon. George Wardrope; the provincial member for Fort William, Hon. C. E. Mapledoram; and the representatives of various groups in the cities. They told us their story. We had a very helpful discussion. Subsequently we have had discussions with officers of the company. Today the Canadian car company has been instructed to proceed immediately with further development of the amphibious tracked personnel carrier known as the Bobcat. This vehicle has been designed by the army and Canadian car company engineers and has attracted military interest in both hemispheres.
This announcement underlines the role the Bobcat may play in future defence plans. Recent tests of three prototype vehicles have established the tactical effectiveness of the
The Address-Mr. Green Bobcat as a defence weapon of the future. This further development will be closely followed by army engineers and defence requirements are being studied.
I point out that this weapon is still in the development stage, but this move is something which has been taken in the hope that it will be of help to the citizens of the lakehead. I have no doubt there will be a statement being made by the officers of the company within the next few hours.
Then I might go on to mention the causeway to Prince Edward Island. There again we expect to have a report in within the next few months, by the end of March.

maintopic: COLUMBIA RIVER-ANNOUNCEMENT OF REFERENCE TO INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smiih (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: COLUMBIA RIVER-ANNOUNCEMENT OF REFERENCE TO INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to make an announcement the text of which has been agreed to by the governments of Canada and the United States for simultaneous release today. This announcement reads as follows:
The governments of the United States and Canada have been engaging in discussions relating to the mutually advantageous development of the waters of the Columbia river basin which cross the boundary.
In the course of these discussions it has seemed desirable to pursue as rapidly as possible the exploration of the various technical problems which bear on the formulation of comprehensive principles. For that purpose and to implement such discussions the governments of Canada and the United States have announced that identical letters were sent today by each government to the two sections of the international joint commission requesting the commission to report specially to governments at an early date its recommendations concerning the principles to be applied in determining:
(a) the benefits which will result from the cooperative use of storage of waters and electrical interconnection within the Columbia river system; and
(b) the apportionment between the two countries of such benefits more particularly in regard to electrical generation and flood control.
This request was made in furtherance of the reference of 1944 to the commission on the Columbia river in order to emphasize the need for an early report from the commission on the specific problem of the allocation of benefits to be derived from the co-operative development of the Columbia river system.
The report of the international Columbia river engineering board will be received by the international joint commission early in March of this year and will be considered at a meeting which will be held in camera in Chicago beginning March 16.
In the meantime, various related matters will continue to be discussed through diplomatic channels.
The letters were delivered by hand this morning to the respective sections of the international joint commission in both capitals, and I think we may rest assured that the commission will report to governments as soon as possible.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, January 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. H. Jorgenson for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson.
(Translation):

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose yesterday evening, I was about to say that, so long as the government persists in procrastinating, the opposition will play its role in this debate; however, we are prepared to vote on the motion right away, and to go on with the business of the nation.
Mr. Speaker, there are many subjects about which I would have liked to deal in the course of my speech, but since my time is about to expire, I shall deal with a subject very much in the news these days: that of our national emblem, which, incidentally, I first advocated in this house, on July 11, 1946. Personally, I am still in favour of a purely Canadian flag, and I hasten to give my reasons for claiming a distinctive flag. Due account must be taken of certain factors which have not yet been pointed out. First, we should remember that a flag should represent, above all, the sovereignty of a country; second, that the sovereignty of a country resides in its parliament which is composed of the Queen, the Senate and the House of Commons. Another point to note is that the place of honour on a flag is in the upper part, near the staff. Thus, the Union Jack represents the sovereignty of the British government, and this is, in any case, what is wanted by some people, in particular the premier of Ontario.
May I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the matter of a national flag is not a responsibility of the province of Ontario or of any other province, but a direct responsibility of the federal government and of the federal parliament.
If, as on the red ensign, the Union Jack on a red background were to remain in the inner upper corner of the flag-therefore, in the place of honour-we would thereby admit the sovereignty of the English parliament over ours, which, to any well-informed person, would seem a formidable mistake, especially since the adoption of the statute of Westminster in 1931, when recognition was given to the sovereignty of Canada and of other commonwealth countries which then had dominion status.

The Address-Mr. Boivin
We should also avoid committing the error of reproducing on this flag, such symbols as the fleur-de-lys, the maple leaf, the beaver, the sheep, or other symbol of any kind.
A flag has nothing to do with a coat of arms: no symbol should be attached to it, because it is, in fact, a recognition of sovereignty.
Generally, the best flags merely consist of three or four bands of colour to which no particular meaning is attached.
I noted during my recent trip to France that the French display with pride and respect the red, white and blue flag of the French republic. Why, for instance, can't we have a simple flag with three or four stripes of colours other than those used by other nations, naturally, and if, in spite of everything, we want to add certain symbols, we could include a white stripe to symbolize the snow which covers our country during half the year, a blue stripe to symbolize the three oceans which surround our continent, a yellow stripe for the golden wheat of the prairies and a red stripe which would symbolize the colour of the uniforms of Wolfe's soldiers, on the Plains of Abraham.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, that would be much better than the thousands of designs suggested to the committee that looked into this matter a few years ago, designs which included all the animals of creation, all the stars in heaven, and as many maple leaves as are found in all the sugar bushes of my province, not to mention lines running from the northwest to the southwest, counter to all concepts of an honourable symbol of a country that glories in the legitimacy of its sovereignty.
Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity to thank all Canadians who submitted to the committee a design of their preferred flag. The contributions were numerous and sincere, which means that, in addition to those people, every true Canadian expects parliament to choose a distinctive flag that will enjoy the place of honour in Canada, the most beautiful country of the world.

speechtext:
Before I commence my remarks on my main theme, Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the many other members of this house in offering my congratulations to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) and the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) upon the excellent speeches they gave in moving and seconding the address in reply. These speeches were positive, constructive and well delivered. The people of their constituencies have every reason to feel proud of the young men they have sent to Ottawa as members of parliament, and who are conducting themselves in such an admirable fashion. Like so many other speeches that have been delivered in this house during this and past sessions by men and women who support the government, these two speeches are indicative of the reason that the Conservative party is today the party of youth as well as the party of the people.
As I said, these speeches were positive and constructive. I only wish I could say the same thing for the next speech we heard in this house, the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). This speech was filled with criticism, and it contained nothing as an alternative to the methods and the measures which the Leader of the Opposition criticized so strongly. Since the Leader of the Opposition had had four months in which to prepare his speech we had been looking forward to a speech which would let us know the Liberal approach to the problems that are facing the country today. We had been expecting, in addition to the normal criticism which one always expects from the Leader of the Opposition and which it is his duty to make, to hear some positive suggestions concerning how the Liberals would run the country if they were the government today. However, the opposition today appears to be just as devoid of positive suggestions as it has been during the past two sessions.
In our democratic form of government, Mr. Speaker, the opposition has two responsibilities. The first responsibility is to oppose, and point out, if it can, the shortcomings of the government and the government's program. The present opposition is trying desperately hard to do this, but they just do not seem to be able to get the proper facts and figures assembled at the one time to enable them to do so. These figures they get from the Martin statistical service continually seem to let them down.
The second duty of an opposition is to demonstrate it can be an alternative government. This the opposition has completely failed to do. They have failed to do it because an alternative government must have a policy,

and this opposition has no policy. We are still waiting to hear how this opposition would improve on the measures which they criticize. They refuse to tell us, simply because they do not know. If they have a policy, let us hear at least some suggestions concerning it. We have heard no suggestions in any of the debates so far.
In his speech on leaders' day the Leader of the Opposition painted a very gloomy picture of our economy, and he tried to depict a state of blue ruin. Of course the Prime Minister in a very kindly way set him straight by pointing out, as recorded on page 58 of Hansard for January 19, 1959, that, in the past year, Canadians worked more, earned more, spent more, and saved more, than in any comparable year in the history of this country. He pointed out also that during the past year, disposable personal income increased by 6.3 per cent; net farm income increased by 22.4 per cent; interest and dividends, and net real income, rose by 6.5 per cent; other disposable income rose by 4.5 per cent; and personal and direct tax declined by 7.8 per cent.
This is the kind of blue ruin the Leader of the Opposition tries so desperately to convince the people of Canada they are suffering from today. That kind of misrepresentation is, I believe, an insult to the people of Canada. The people of Canada today are not accepting it any more than they did last March. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, when referring to last March I am reminded of the fact that one senior Liberal the other day made what I considered a very sensible suggestion. He suggested that perhaps we could make our humane slaughter legislation retroactive to March 31 last. I think that might be a good suggestion.
If these prophets of doom and gloom would get out of their offices, get away from the crepe they keep hanging around their shoulders and around their speeches, and get out across the country where they could talk to the businessmen, farmers, fishermen and lumbermen, the people who really make this country go, then they would learn something. What they would learn would be that the people of this country have a great deal of confidence in this country's economy, in this government, and particularly in our Prime Minister. The people of this country are confident that our economy is going to continue to move steadily forward. They are confident of that because they know this economy is soundly based. They are planning, they are building, and they are expanding. They have confidence and faith in the future of this country even if the members of the opposition have not.
The Address-Mr. Hees
I think the kind of criticism and condemnation of the economy of the country that we have been hearing so often in this house from members of the opposition is serving no good purpose. It is simply inconsistent with the facts. They would do a great deal better if they started boosting instead of knocking and started helping the people of this country do the excellent job they are doing in moving this country's economy forward.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it would do a great deal of good for these men of little faith if they would speak, for instance, to the people who are putting hundreds of millions of dollars into the iron ore development in the Ungava bay region. Those people do not lack confidence in Canada's future. It would do them good to talk to the private investors who propose to spend $10 million this year in investigating and developing oil and gas prospects in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon. Those people do not lack confidence in the economy of this country. They have plenty of it. It would do them good to talk, as I did a few nights ago, to the executives of a Canadian steel company which is going to spend $28 million on an expansion program in the next ten months. They have no lack of confidence in the economy of this country; they have tremendous confidence in it. Their facts and figures show that the economy of this country is going ahead, and that is why they are building to keep pace with its expansion.
That is the spirit of confidence, Mr. Speaker, that is pervading our whole economy. It is pervading everybody, with the exception of the members of the official opposition. They are too busy waiting around day after day, hoping that some larger unemployment figures are going to be produced so they can gloat over them. If they would start getting positive and stop being negative they would be doing a great deal better job as members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, who are supposed to be working for the betterment of the whole of Canada.
Let us now turn, Mr. Speaker, from the negative and destructive side, as depicted by what the opposition is saying, to the positive and constructive side, as represented by what the government is doing. I should like to give three examples of what a department of this government is doing, as all departments of this government are doing, to further our national development program. As we all know national development, particularly in a country the size of Canada, requires tremendous transportation facilities, to assist free enterprise in developing and expanding the economy. In developing the country we need three most important things

The Address-Mr. Hees in the way of transportation facilities, namely airfields, harbours and ships, including both icebreakers and supply ships. In the last election, the Leader of the Opposition scoffed at and made great fun of our development program. As you will well recall, Mr. Speaker, he described it as simply a program of building roads from igloo to igloo. He said that we were doing no more than had the former Liberal administration.
I should like to give comparative figures for the three categories of national development I have mentioned, namely shipbuilding, airfields and the building of harbours. I am going to compare what is being done today by this government with what was done by the former Liberal government in the last year in which they were in office, namely the fiscal year 1956-57. First of all, in the development of airfields and air terminals, in the year 1956-57 the Liberal government spent $22 million. It built four terminals and completed 26 runways. In this present year we are spending $56 million and will complete six terminals and 37 runways. In other words we are doing approximately two and a half times what the former government did in a comparable period when they were in office.
Then let us turn to the question of developing harbours.

We have a program of development at the lakehead which the hon. member knows about very well indeed, and which I think he will agree is a farsighted, comprehensive, and adequate program, and one which will do a first class job for the lake-head. If he has any contrary opinions may I say that it is the first time he has expressed to me anything except complete approval of the plans the government has for the developing of harbour facilities at the lakehead.

I think I have clearly demonstrated what we are doing, and why we are doing it. We do things constructively, instead of just talking destructively; the only thing the opposition seems able to do. We believe in providing the necessary transportation facilities to assist free enterprise in doing the job it has done for the past 100 years, and which has developed the economy of the country. We believe in providing these facilities to the greatest possible degree that we can. We are providing these transportation facilities, not only to help the economy in the southern regions of the country, but to develop the vast wealth in our northern regions as well.
This program is consistent with what has always been the policy of this party as far as developing the country is concerned. Nearly 100 years ago our first great Conservative prime minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, saw very clearly the need for providing transportation facilities in the form of a great transcontinental railway to make it possible for free enterprise to develop the country from east to west. Today, we are fortunate in having another great Conservative prime minister who sees with equal clearness the need for providing transportation facilities of a modern character to enable free enterprise to complete the job, and develop the country from south to north.
