speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) who has just taken his seat, I too wish to join our colleagues in extending congratulations to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Hut I am in good company with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) when I say that if my remarks must of necessity be brief they are none the less very sincere.
I should like to address myself very briefly to three matters, one of which was included in the speech from the throne, one of which was not included in the speech from the throne and which I respectfully submit should have been dealt with, and the third a matter that has evolved during this debate. The first matter I should like to refer to is the bill of rights and human freedoms of the Prime Minister. I consider that this measure will be welcomed and is welcomed by the entire country. It can become a Canadian Magna Carta; and because it can become that I should like to point out that in being reduced to writing there is a danger that it might tend to circumscribe or limit the freedoms and the human rights which are now enjoyed.
For that reason I say that the government should exercise the greatest caution possible

The Address-Mr. Crestohl and do everything in its power to make certain that all viewpoints are heard and all ideas are expressed and included in a document that will in truth be a charter of human rights. There might be some danger if we do not take these precautions.
Canada has been described as a mosaic of minorities, and that is true. There are different points of view, different cultures, different backgrounds, all of which must be very carefully considered to make sure that the mosaic will be fully represented in our Canadian charter. Therefore I want to support as ardently as I can the suggestion of my leader that a parliamentary committee composed of members of both houses of parliament be appointed in order to study all the angles, all the problems, all the points of view before we finally circumscribe and enclose within a framework the fundamental freedoms and human rights which Canadians now and in the future may enjoy. Let us make certain that everything is included, because once the charter is reduced to writing it can become quite a dangerous document.
I suggest that first of all the government should invite legal experts, professors of law at the universities, sociologists, church and religious leaders and labour leaders, and certainly they should invite the provinces. It is my suggestion that perhaps the provincial attorneys general should be summoned by the government to a conference, because there are conflicts of opinion with respect to whether or not the constitutional phase will be adequately covered. At the present time there is a growing fear, a growing anxiety in the country, that perhaps all the constitutional difficulties will not be overcome and that some of the rights which the Canadian parliament may suggest may come into conflict with provincial rights. A meeting with the provinces may perhaps produce some agreement that will result in the constitutional difficulties between the federal and provincial authorities being solved.
Therefore I urge the Prime Minister as strongly as I can that such a conference be convened. We are at the present time and have been deluged by recommendations from various representative Canadian organizations. We should not ignore the representations they make. We now read in the newspapers, or hear over the radio and television, articles and announcements by authorities on constitutional law which seriously question whether such a bill of rights would do the good it is intended to do or whether it would do harm, and I therefore suggest that it would be a great mistake for the Prime Minister not to exercise every possible precaution to make sure that his bill will be what it is intended to be.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Are you for it or against it?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Everybody, I think, is for
it, but we are anxious to make sure that the Prime Minister will not have relied entirely on the advice he is now getting from his cabinet or from hon. members opposite but that he should seek advice from the entire country; from men who are students of sociology and men who are students of constitutional law; people who are as deeply concerned about the future of Canadians as the hon. member is and as I am.
My suggestion is a purely constructive one, and I will carry it further. This proposed measure will in all probability be adorned with the royal assent given by Her Majesty the Queen in person, and because it is a measure which will be sanctioned by Her Majesty herself I plead with the Prime Minister that he convene such a committee as I have suggested. After all, we have convened all sorts of committees in the past. Quite recently a committee was set up by parliament to study humane methods of slaughtering animals. I think hon. members opposite would agree with me that it would be ironic and incongruous if we were to appoint a committee to study how animals should die and not appoint a committee to study how humans should live.
The second topic on which I should like to touch is the question of immigration. I think the whole country accepts the fact that the people of Canada are the most valuable natural resource we have, and consequently I was disappointed that no reference was made in the speech from the throne to the question of immigration. The importance of immigration has been continually stressed by leading Canadians and quite recently by three authorities who will, I know, be acceptable to hon. members opposite. I refer to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Immigration herself. I should like, for the information of the house, to read what the Prime Minister himself said on April 27, 1957 about immigrants and immigration while he was making one of his tours. I quote from the Toronto Globe and Mail:
At his first stop of the day-a conference with the ethnic press association in Toronto-Mr. Diefenbaker filled in the detail of one aspect of that program. Development, he told the editors of foreign language publications, demands manpower. The only way to meet the needs for skill and talents is through accelerated immigration.
Mr. Speaker, I underscore the words "accelerated immigration". The Prime Minister said further:
A government formed by the Conservatives, he added, will undertake an intensive immigration policy that will make available to all sections of the country those talents and skills.

And here I underscore the word "intensive". He said the party would undertake an intensive immigration policy, not, I would point out, a retarded immigration policy.
Now I turn to my second authority who, as I said, will also no doubt be acceptable to hon. members opposite, namely the Minister of Finance, who on Tuesday, June 17, 1958 is reported at page 1231 of Hansard to have said:
Population growth of itself does not ensure progress, but in a country such as ours it has a special significance. It provides a greater market for our agricultural produce and for the products of our factories and reduces our vulnerability to changes in external demand. It brings us a greater diversity of talent and the means of employing it to better advantage. It reduces the per capita cost of supplying essential services in this great land. There can be no doubt-
And I underscore the words "no doubt"-
-that the population growth of the post-war period has had these effects.
And now I turn to my third authority, no less a person than the minister of immigration herself, who is reported as follows in the Montreal Star of January 14, 1959:
Immigration minister Ellen Fairclough said today that immigrants have helped to bolster the Canadian economy by their consumer buying, by establishing new businesses and industry and by bringing money into the country.
Mrs. Fairclough denied that immigrants were taking jobs away from native-born workers.
These are very significant words, Mr. Speaker, and I wish to underline them. Then the report continues:
Mrs. Fairclough also noted that during the eight-year period 1950-58 immigrants purchased 3,879 farms and rented 849 others.
"The purchasing power of the immigrants is reflected in such purchases during the 1951-58 period as 173,000 electric or gas stoves, more than 150,000 refrigerators and more than 128,000 washing machines," she said.
"In the last 12 years immigrants have brought into this country more than $800 million in cash and securities and some $300 million in effects. In 1957 alone, they paid an estimated $190 million in direct taxes," she continued.
These are clear statements of policy by the Prime Minister, by the Minister of Finance and by the minister of immigration herself.
My leader earlier in this debate spoke of contradictions, confusion and instability in many phases of government. Let me point out some very poignant cases of confusion, contradiction and instability which have occurred with regard to the government's immigration policy. I would draw to the attention of the house that the Prime Minister's glorious recommendation of an accelerated immigration policy was made in April, 1957, just prior to the election of that year.
A little over a month after that election press reports stated the following as a matter
The Address-Mr. Crestohl of government policy, and I now quote from the Ottawa Citizen of July 27, 1957. This is the quotation:
The Progressive Conservative government in a major policy announcement has placed restrictions on immigration into Canada for the balance of 1957.
For the rest of the year immigrants arriving for open placement on the labour market-those with no prearranged work contracts-have a July 31 deadline for arrival.
That was the first announcement made immediately after the election. Another press release on the same subject which appeared in the Toronto Telegram of July 27, 1957 reads:
Confronted by rising unemployment and scarcity of winter housing, the Diefenbaker government last night placed heavy restrictions on immigration for the rest of this year.
Hon. E. Davie Fulton, acting immigration minister, announced that after July 31 only persons with guaranteed jobs or financially-responsible relatives already here, will be admitted.
That was corroborated and confirmed by another responsible minister of the government, the Minister of Labour, some three months later when he said on October 16, 1957, as reported at page 29 of Hansard of that date:
I might say also, on behalf of the government, that we have curtailed for the balance of the year the influx of immigrants which swelled our total labour population.
What a contradiction of what the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration had said. One minister said that immigrants do not interfere with employment or take jobs from native Canadians, and the other minister in direct contradiction said the opposite.
I should like to trace for a moment the results of the immigration policy of this government. Two or three months before the election the Prime Minister made an appeal for open door immigration, and I believe he was sincere in what he said which was designed to win the vote of the ethnic group. I know he favours large immigration into Canada. No one, not even I who both in and out of season have pleaded for an open door policy for immigration, could have improved upon the statements to this effect made by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the Minister of Finance before the 1957 election. No one could have made more eloquent speeches. Yet the moment the election was over we heard from the acting minister of immigration a statement which like that made by the Minister of Labour almost categorically denied what had been said by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance with respect to an open door policy for immigration. Is this not a clear cut illustration of

The Address-Mr. Crestohl confusion and contradiction? Where is the policy of this government with respect to immigration?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They were just carrying out the Liberal policy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Let me tell you how they were carrying out the Liberal policy. The Liberal policy brought into Canada hundreds of thousands of immigrants. The present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration herself has outlined what these immigrants have done for Canada. How can the hon. member who interrupted say that his government carried out the Liberal immigration policy, when the figures tell a different story? If the hon. member does not know what he is talking about let him refer to the facts and figures.
I am always pleased at interruptions, Mr. Speaker. When I first came to this house I was told that if no one interrupted you when you were making a speech it indicated that no one was interested in what you were saying and you were making no impression. To that extent interruptions are symbols of interest; and if you were interrupted by hon. members opposite it indicated that you were saying things that hurt them. I am grateful to the hon. member who has just interrupted for indicating in this way that the deficiencies in the immigration policies of his government which I am pointing out and the horrible series of contradictions are a source of concern to him. What I am saying has hit home and hurts.
Let me read another interesting statement which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of January 5, 1959. In addressing the Oshawa Rotary club the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration released some figures of interest. The report reads in part:
The year's immigration total was less than half 1957's 282,164 and less than the 1946-56 10-year average of 126,000.
Here we have a statement by a minister of the government disclosing the fact that total immigration in 1958 was less than half that of 1957. It seems almost to have been said with a sense of pride in contradiction to former statements made by the hon. lady.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question. Who signed the directive reducing immigration into Canada in June of that year before the Conservative government took office?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There was no cut in immigration other than that announced by the present Minister of Justice, who was then acting minister of immigration. He explained that the government reduced the flow of immigration into Canada as a first step to meet the problem of unemployment. I do not know

to what extent he exposed or embarrassed the Prime Minister, who had spoken in favour of an open door policy for immigration before the election, particularly when he was pleading for the support of the ethnic groups in this country.
As I said, the article from which I read is a clear indication that immigration was reduced by one half in the period of a year. Because the Minister of Labour had said that the government stopped the flow of immigration in order not to interfere with the employment of Canadians one might assume that there would have been a corresponding reduction in unemployment in the last year, but the facts do not bear this out. Unemployment increased despite the reduction in immigration. I therefore go along with the statement made by the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration who said clearly that in her judgment and in the judgment of many eminent sociologists and economists immigration into Canada in no way interfered with employment.
Let me read some comments by the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration as reported in the Regina Leader Post of January 17, 1959:
Justice Minister Davie Fulton was the first to express his views . . . Mr. Fulton said one of the first decisions, an unpleasant one, the Conservative administration had to take was to curb the flow of immigration which had been going on at the rate of 300,000 a year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That was a Liberal decision.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
You are perfectly right. Under the Liberal administration 300,000 immigrants a year were coming to Canada, but that was too much for the present government. The Minister of Justice made a further statement, reported in the same article as follows:
If the flow had not been curbed, he said, the majority would have come seeking jobs and finding none. They would be "competing with Canadians for a shrinking labour opportunity".
In the same article the stand taken by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is commented on as follows:
Mrs. Fairclough took a slightly different tack. She said that year by year immigration brings to Canada a steady flow of producers as well as consumers of Canadian products. In a very real sense, she said, a new and important domestic market is being created by immigrants.
Now Mrs. Fairclough introduced her seemingly contradictory thoughts to what Mr. Fulton had been saying. ... In good times little criticism of immigration is heard. But when economic expansion slows down, there is a tendency on the part of some to question the value of immigration. Occasionally we hear that immigrants take work from native-born Canadians and aggravate unemployment; this notwithstanding the oft-expressed view of reputable economists that there is little or no connection between immigration and unemployment.

Here you have it, Mr. Speaker. Three responsible ministers of the cabinet, including the Prime Minister, take one tack on immigration; speak very eloquently in favour of large immigration, accelerated immigration to Canada; point out and emphasize the value of immigrants to Canada, what they have contributed in the past to Canada; and within a matter of weeks three other responsible ministers take an entirely different tack. They say, curb immigration, stop immigration, and they contradict the statement of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration that immigrants do not interfere with employment. What clearer example could one possibly give of contradiction, confusion and instability in government policy? I refer only to its immigration policy.
I would suggest the Minister of Labour has his problems to worry about, and therefore he announces on behalf of the government a reduction in the number of immigrants. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has her problems to worry about. She favours immigration. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, it is a case of the right hand in the cabinet not knowing what its left hand is doing, and that confirms the clear-cut statement of the Leader of the Opposition that there is confusion and contradiction in the government; particularly, as I have just pointed out, with respect to immigration.
I should like to make some observations on the feature of this debate, Mr. Speaker, which was emphasized over and over again by government speakers who are constantly nudging the opposition with the question, "What do you suggest; what would you do about it?" We can understand, of course, from the contradictions which are so apparent and so obvious that there could be cause for great concern among the members of the government. This is obvious, Mr. Speaker. It is clearly the result of^ inexperience. If government spokesmen would rise in their places in the house and simply say with all candor and all sincerity, "We have just taken charge of the government; we are new in this; we believe we have policies which we shall develop, but we have not had the experience, and therefore at the beginning of our administration there may be some apparent confusion, some apparent contradiction, but it will straighten itself out", I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that would be a becoming statement; it would be in line with the facts.
I suggest they should do this rather than try with great difficulty to defend all this confusion. We would have great respect for a government which would say to the country, "We have a program, we have a
The Address-Mr. Crestohl policy which we will implement, but give us an opportunity. We have not had the vast experience the former government had after 22 years of power. They were tried and experienced. We will perform just as well in time." To have failed to make that statement is in my judgment a gross oversight.
Then they say to the opposition, "What would you suggest?" "What should we do?" Well, Mr. Speaker, to nudge the opposition with these questions is a little bit ludicrous. Let us look at it. Politics being politics, will anyone say that a government will do those things which an opposition suggests? Oh, it is just so much beautiful language, so much challenging language. It is another way of saying, "We don't know what to do; what would you suggest?" When our leader makes a suggestion to the government-and he made it again recently-that a drastic cut in income tax be made so there would be more take-home pay in every employee's envelope, there would be more money thrown into circulation and more buying power and this buying power would create more production and more production would create more labour opportunities and unemployment would be reduced, what is the result? It was a practical suggestion, but it was completely ignored. It was not argued against; it was not set aside; it was just completely ignored. But they persist in asking the opposition, "What would you suggest?"
Then, Mr. Speaker, in my humble way I myself had the temerity to suggest to the government a 30-day or a 60-day sales tax holiday. That, too, would throw more money into circulation. People would be inclined to purchase; people would have more funds and would buy within this 30- or 60-day period because they would know that within that period they could purchase without having to pay sales tax. There would be an impetus to buying; buying power would be increased; production again would be increased and unemployment would be reduced. But that, too, was completely ignored even though it did have editorial support.
I would dare answer that question which is constantly put to the opposition, "What would you do?" by taking a page from history, indeed from Canadian history. What did other governments do? What did another government do at a time when the country found itself in a difficult economic condition. In fact, Mr. Speaker, our economic position is so serious today that I in any event and all hon. members should shudder at the thought that now for the second time within my memory Canadians are humbled to such an extent that they must seek food in bread lines and from free soup kitchens.

The Address-Mr. Crestohl
Immediately after the first world war, in the years 1919, 1920 and 1921, as a young man I had the sad and heartbreaking experience of seeing bread lines and soup kitchens in Montreal. And now, as I said, for the second time within my memory we learn from the press that bread lines and soup kitchens have been established in Toronto and Vancouver. This is a sad thing for us as members of parliament, representing the people, to contemplate; and I have reason to fear that this state of affairs may even spread to other cities. I urge that it is the solemn duty of members of parliament, the spokesmen of the people of Canada, regardless of political party or affiliation, to give this matter the serious consideration it deserves.
I say, Mr. Speaker, the government has the power to arrest this spreading calamity. All it needs is the courage, and courage means not to seek to do only those things which are popular or popular vote-catchers. All it needs is the courage to do those things which are necessary and urgent regardless of whether they are popular and will catch votes. It is the duty of the government to place the re-sponsibilty, the urgency and the needs of our people above political party politics. This has been done by another government.
Before I even touch on that matter I should point out that both in the 1919 and 1920 eras, when we had soup kitchens and bread lines, just as they are developing now in our country, peculiarly the governments were Conservative governments. I do not make that as an accusation but as a statement of fact. It may be sheer coincidence or perhaps, as someone has said, the Conservative party is just a hard-luck party. It is a horrible picture to contemplate, Mr. Speaker.
I say to hon. members that it may be unpopular to do certain things, but they must be done. It may be quite true, I quite understand and sympathize, that hon. gentlemen opposite even feel politically pained by this sad picture; their humane sensibilities may also be pained. However, they should stop playing painful politics, because that is what is happening. Every measure, everything that is said by the government has only one objective: Is it popular? Will it get us votes? They should not be concerned with these things so early in the administration of the government.
The Prime Minister sees visions and I too, Mr. Speaker, see visions. When I think of these bread lines, the playing of politics, the doing of only those things which are popular, then the vision I see is that of Nero and Rome.
As I said a moment ago, at another time when this country was facing a serious

economic situation another political party did things which were not very popular. If we go back to 1939, 1940 and 1941, when rigid controls were set up in this country, we find that they were not popular with anyone. They were good for the country. They may have been bad for a political party but they were necessary for the good of the country. We all recall the so-called dollar a year brigade which was pressed into service by the then government. Irrespective of the political party to which these gentlemen belonged they were summoned to the service of Canada. Canada needed their help at the time. It is quite clear that they came forward, and the government of the day did not hesitate to introduce those rigid controls, those unpopular measures. There were price controls, salary controls, rent controls and so on.
I am not suggesting these as measures the government should adopt today. I am simply pointing them out and saying they were unpopular measures that were adopted by a government which did not think of its political future but thought of its country's future. All these controls were set up, as I said, and men were summoned from all parts of Canada, irrespective of their political allegiance.

I had not intended this morning, Mr. Speaker, to touch on the subject of immigration. However, having listened carefully to the remarks of the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) I cannot help but point out to him that what he has been criticizing at considerable length in the way of immigration policy was, in fact, the policy of his own government. The policy of the previous Liberal government on immigration-and in my view it was not a bad policy though not always well carried out-was to regulate the flow of immigrants so that it was in keeping with the economic situation in this country. We do not want to bring in people for whom there is no housing or for whom there is no work. I will take second place to no one as an advocate of an active and full immigration policy for Canada.
However, as the hon. member pointed out in the latter part of his speech, we have had economic difficulties. It is known that many immigrants, in their first years in this country, have difficulties because their knowledge of the languages of Canada is sometimes not good enough to get them the best type of employment. Very often they are the ones upon whom economic difficulties fall most heavily. The hon. member for Cartier was suggesting, it seemed to me, that we should have brought in large numbers of people to walk the streets of this country and be a charge upon the communities in which they live, and to start out in this country in a very unhappy frame of mind. The policy of cutting back on immigration, as was pointed out by someone on this side of the house, was inaugurated by a Liberal government before the election in 1957, when they sent notices to the immigration offices throughout the world to be prepared to cut down on immigration as the economic outlook was not good.
This government, as has been shown by the speeches of the Prime Minister and other ministers, is a believer in immigration, but a believer in sound immigration. We believe in bringing people to this country when we are able to give them jobs, give them housing and give them a good start toward becoming Canadians. That is the policy of the government, and that is the policy that has been carried out. The hon. member mentioned that last year immigration was considerably lower than the previous year. What he did not mention was that immigration the previous year was the greatest since before the first war. Immigration last year compares very favourably with many of the years since the war when the policy was administered by the former Liberal government.
I come, Mr. Speaker, from the riding of St. Lawrence-St. George. It is the very centre
The Address-Mr. Chambers of the metropolis of Canada. Many of our citizens work in other ridings, and many of the people who work in our riding live in other ridings. It is therefore difficult for me to speak specifically of St. Lawrence-St. George. We are part of a larger community, and we are affected by the problems of that larger community. Apart from that, having listened to and read in Hansard the speeches of the various hon. members who have preceded me, I have noted that they have taken unto their own ridings all the compliments that can be bestowed upon a riding in Canada-I should say, all but one. speechtext:
I make no exception. As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, we are involved in the problems of a larger community. One of the problems facing the city of Montreal today is transportation across the St. Lawrence river. We in Montreal are grateful to the government and to the Minister of Transport for the efforts that are being made to alleviate that problem. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) has been greatly interested in the problem of the Victoria bridge which is to be partially closed for alterations by the Canadian National Railways. Since we on this side of the house have been asking for constructive suggestions I thought I might ask the hon. member for Laurier whether he could not make a constructive suggestion in this regard. As everyone knows he was closely concerned with the seaway and with transportation generally in the past. In the Montreal Star of November 1, 1954 we find the following statement:
The chairman of the seaway authority, Mr. Chevrier, has announced that a formula has been found to avoid delays on Victoria bridge once the Montreal end of the seaway project has been completed. He will not say now what it is.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, this his silence has gone on long enough, and that if he knows how to keep the bridge open and still do the necessary alterations, now is the time when he should let us all in on the secret rather than simply ask the Minister of Transport questions in that regard.
In this debate the charge of the opposition seems to be that the government is confused. But, Mr. Speaker, there can be no more confusion than that which is indicted in the speeches that have come from the opposition benches. I do not want to go over all the ground, but I should like to take just one speech I heard. It was not made in this house but was made on the national radio

The Address-Mr. Chambers network by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). I was interested the other day to hear him rise to make a correction in Hansard, at which time he said that he did not jive but that he jibed, and went on to clear up the point by explaining how he was using the term. When he first mentioned the term I, of course, thought that as he was an old nautical man it had to do with the well known phrase in sailing, namely to jibe, which is to go about before the wind. May I say that there is no one who spends more time before the wind than the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
He began his remarks by very kindly saying that he and his party did not hold the Conservative government responsible for unemployment but that what they held the government responsible for was the fact that the government had done absolutely nothing about it; and then he jibed. He started to talk about inflation. He said that inflation was a very serious problem and that everything the government had done served to increase inflation. A moment or two previously he had said that the government had done nothing. Then he said that everything they had done was inflationary.
It is possible, in fact probable, that some of the actions of the government to alleviate the unemployment situation were inflationary. But what the hon. member failed to tell us was which of those measures he would have preferred the government had not put into effect. Was it the extension of unemployment insurance that he did not want because it was inflationary? Was it the housing program that has given work to thousands and thousands of Canadians during a difficult period? Was that what he did not want put into effect because it was inflationary? Was it the public works program, the building of roads to the north or the improvement of our harbours? Were those the things that he felt should not have been done because they were inflationary? He did not say, Mr. Speaker. However, I can suggest some things the government may have been considering which no doubt would be inflationary and which perhaps now should be dropped.
During the last session the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate took us on a magnificent tour through that riding of his, in the course of which he stopped at every harbour and community, every pile of logs and every place where there was a pile of logs ten years ago. In each and every one of those corners he found that some public work was necessary. Here it was a new dock, there a cold storage plant or some place to tie up his ship. If those works were now undertaken I suggest that they would be extremely

inflationary, and probably would cause damage not only to the country but particularly to Bonavista-Twillingate.
Yesterday the hon. member for Port Arthur had something to say comparing our economy with that of communist countries. I want to make it clear right away that I am not suggesting that I think he was favouring that type of economy. However, he pointed out, and with some truth, that in those countries there is disciplined society, and that because of the disciplined society and because the efforts of every citizen can be directed, there is there an efficiency that we perhaps do not possess. This may be one of the reasons that they get their rockets closer to the moon than do the western countries.
I do not think there is anyone in this house who wants a disciplined society in exchange for our free society, and I think there are few in this country who do. Nevertheless we are in competition with the communist countries, and we must find-and I think we have done so-a substitute for this iron discipline. We must find some method of mobilizing the efforts of our people while maintaining their freedom.
To you, Mr. Speaker, and to all other hon. members I suggest that in the sense of national purpose that has been instilled into the great majority of our people by the Prime Minister we have the substitute for discipline. Today we have a country that is united as it has seldom been in its history. It is united because the people of this country believe in the program of the government. They believe in the qualities of leadership that exist in those who occupy the front benches of the Conservative party.
As the hon. member for Port Arthur pointed out, in our society there are some activities which he described as not being vital parts of production, and he named one or two. I think you could define those people who use the resources of this country solely for their own profit and without any consideration for the national purpose as doing something which is contrary to the long-term aspirations of our people. As I say, he named a couple; I could name a couple more, including those persons who take up time and newsprint to do such things as to print obscene publications and persons who use time, effort and capital to do what I would call useless things such as printing the social register.
Then we come to those whose profit is not in money but in political capital, people such as some who have spoken in this debate who will use anything they can put their finger on to turn a political profit without any consideration of the effect their words will have on the people of the country. This has been pointed out before in this debate, but when we

have members opposite stand up and say that the country is going to the dogs, that there is no direction, no future, they may make a short term political profit but what in effect they are doing is damaging the confidence of the people of the country.
People who are considering investment in employment-producing industries, people who are considering setting up new firms to develop our natural resources may feel, because these respected gentlemen say the future is dark that they should not do so at this time. So it seems to me that these people, together with those whose only consideration is monetary profit, are what you might call the negative part of our society at this time.
We on this side of the house have been criticized because occasionally we say that we support the Conservative Prime Minister. I do not know why this should be. If we say anything in favour of our Prime Minister it is suggested that we are looking for advancement only, but I make no apology. If I did not support the Prime Minister I would not be sitting on this side of the house. We follow his leadership because it is the best leadership in Canada today. It has been ably demonstrated in this debate, in the speech from the throne and by the accomplishments of the government since it came into office the year before last that we have in the Prime Minister a leader in whom the vast majority of the people of the country have confidence. It is he who has pointed out to the people of the country the national purpose of which I spoke. He has pictured to them the destiny of the country, and he is leading them along the path of progress toward that destiny.
I only want to say one other thing, Mr. Speaker, and it has to do with parliament. A year or two ago we used to hear speeches on the rights of parliament and the rights of members of parliament. One of the main planks of the Conservative platform was to restore the rights of parliament, and today we no longer hear such speeches. We no longer hear complaints from the opposition that their rights are being withheld. In fact if there are any breaches of the rights of the house they still come from the opposition. I feel sorry for them. I know they are reduced in number, but I suggest to them that the way to increase their number is not by bringing their friends into the house without having them first elected.
Let them do as the Prime Minister and other members of the government have suggested. Let them bring forward constructive policies. Let them say to the people of Canada something that will lead the people to believe that they have come back from the bankruptcy of policy which put them out of office. Let them
The Address-Mr. Michaud look over the constructive, forward-looking, far-reaching program of the government and learn their lesson from it.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join at this time with those hon. members who have preceded me in this debate by extending my sincere congratulations to the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Jorgenson) on the able manner in which he discharged his duty.
(Translation):
I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) who, in seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne, did very well. He was a credit to his electors and his constituency.
I should like also to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to express my satisfaction of the fact that, this session again, you are Speaker of this house.
It had not been my intention, Mr. Speaker, to speak on the subject of immigration at this time. But after hearing cabinet ministers, and particularly the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers), who complained this morning about the former Liberal government's immigration policy, I could not resist the temptation to remind the house of a few facts and incidents relating to that matter.
Allow me to quote from a few newspaper articles I have on my desk. Here is, for example, what one could read on February 15, 1955, in the paper La Presse under the title:
Conservatives want to boost immigration-Mr. Davie Fulton introduced a non confidence motion and advocated more active recruiting in Great Britain.
Note, Mr. Speaker, that if the non confidence motion had carried, it would have caused the fall of the Liberal government.
And the article adds:
The government's immigration policy is neither clear, nor consistent nor integrated. It does not meet the needs of Canada. It does not live up to the responsibilities of Canada. Its implementation involves discrimination against Canadians and non-Canadians.

Opposition-

-urges more immigrants.

(Text):
I think it is appropriate to state at this time that the debate now engaging the retention of the house has clearly indicated the seriousness of the many problems now confronting the Canadian nation. It also has shown the confusion, embarrassment and indecision which the government is displaying in dealing with these many problems. But what else could be expected? It has been said that the government promised its way to power. Now it is indicted for its dismal failure to implement its election promises.
Perhaps it would be proper to recall to the government that never before was the old French adage so true: "Qui seme le vent, recolte la tempete." How well I remember the fantastic promises made in my own riding by the supporters of the present government in the course of the last two election campaigns-jobs of their own choosing for all those who would support the present government's candidate; pensions to all within the age limit of the Old Age Assistance Act; more generous unemployment insurance benefits to the unemployed with or without the required number of insurance stamps. Public works projects were promised on every corner, even invading the field of private enterprise. Factories were promised for every village, and the provincial field was also brought into the picture during the campaign. New roads, paved if need be, were promised in every section of the county of Kent. Then came the chorus of "being on the winning side" with all its overtones 

of accompanying skull duggery regardless of how incompatible it was with all the concepts of democratic principles, the suggestion that unless you are on the winning side you cannot expect the same benefits and the same privileges.
If one recognizes that the pattern followed in my own riding was much the same as that followed throughout the whole country by Conservative spokesmen, it is little wonder that the chickens are now coming home to roost in such large numbers. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the main causes of the government's present embarrassment are of its own making and the direct result of this unbridled flow of irresponsible promises which overwhelmed all media of publicity in the last two political campaigns. It is therefore the responsibility of the government and not the responsibility of the opposition, as has been so often suggested by government speakers in this debate, to meet all the expectancies aroused by its own supporters, let alone its own candidates.
Much has been said about unemployment during the course of this debate. I have no intention at this time of going into details concerning this matter. Numerous statistics have been quoted and many arguments have been advanced as to who should bear the responsibility for the present unemployment situation. However, my duty compels me at this time to say to this house that unemployment with all it comprises in terms of moral and physical suffering is far too prevalent in my own constituency.
Before leaving for Ottawa for the present session I saw cases of want and poverty that would wring your heart, cases of children without food or clothing, homes without fuel, situations that are a challenge to our democratic and Christian institutions. Statistics will never reveal the true picture of the economic conditions existing in the constituency I represent. There are an untold number of workers who are unable to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits due to their inability last year, through no fault of their own, to earn the minimum number of stamps required, 15.
Numerous excerpts have been read from the statement of His Eminence Cardinal Leger on the subject of unemployment during recent days. I wish to cite one more extract from that timely and most important appeal:
The wealth of a country is measured by the distribution of material goods rather than by the abundance of these goods. A people which does not enjoy a just distribution of material riches-no matter how abundant these riches are-must be considered a poor people in a rich country.
One of the main causes of unemployment in my part of the country is the present

slump which affects the lumber industry. Thousands of men formerly employed in the manufacture of our pulp and lumber are now sitting idle due to lack of demand. Where pulpwood used to sell at from $15 to $17 a cord at roadside it is now sold at $8 to $10 a cord if indeed you are lucky enough to sell a few cords. The price is hardly more than the stumpage costs.
A further drawback to the pulp industry was the recent freight rate increase. Shippers have told me that this increase means an additional cost, depending upon the delivery point, of $3 to $3.40 a cord. We are told by the government that equalizing measures will be adopted to relieve producers' goods from the eastern and western parts of the country from the paralysing effects of the new freight rate increase. Efforts should be made to make these measures applicable to wood shipments along with other goods.
Mention should also be made of the recent action of the New Brunswick government with regard to woods operations by lumber companies of that province. Through arbitrary measures imposed upon these companies they are now obliged to cut on their leased lands larger quantities of wood than they would normally cut, thus curtailing the production of the small private supplier such as the farmer and settler.
These are all matters which should receive careful study from all parties concerned with a view to promoting renewed activity in the woods industry, which represents a segment of prime importance in the general economy in the province of New Brunswick.
There is one other aspect of the over-all labour field in the maritimes which is different from the situation which existed during past years. As a matter of fact, during the last five or six years two projects of major proportions absorbed the surplus available labour force which was not otherwise locally employed. I refer to the construction of Camp Gagetown in New Brunswick and the construction of air bases in Labrador. But it now seems that these two projects are nearing completion and therefore will not provide the same opportunities for employment as in the past. This situation should be corrected, if mass unemployment is to be avoided in the maritimes, by the launching of new projects of the same wide scope as those I have mentioned. Projects of these proportions were also suggested by my colleague the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. McWilliam.)
Without, then, elaborating on their advisability I submit that the government should seriously consider the construction of a causeway between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island and the construction of the
The Address-Mr. Michaud Chignecto canal. The undertaking of these works would bring about the double advantage of creating a wide field of local employment for our working force as well as fostering a wider development of our commercial and industrial life.
Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to hear during the reading of the throne speech the government's intention of reviewing farm credit. The following words appear in the speech from the throne:
You will also be invited to make a comprehensive review and revision of the legislation concerning farm credit, in order that credit may be more effective in assisting in the development and maintenance of an efficient and prosperous agriculture.
The matter of farm credit is one of great concern to all those whose responsibility it is to guide agriculture at the present time. Farm groups, farm leaders and farm technical advisers, nearly all are agreed that the emphasis should be placed on larger farm units in order to reduce the cost of farm operation and increase net farm revenue.
Great interest in farm practices is emerging in the maritime provinces at this time. I should like at this time to read from a news report in the Moncton Daily Times of January 19 last:
Proper Use of Land said Fundamental-
Atlantic provinces farmers "must change their methods drastically to meet needed changes in production pointed out by agricultural research, changing marketing practices and changing consumer demands," declared Dr. Frank MacKinnon, Charlottetown, president of the Atlantic provinces economic council, in a Moncton address Saturday.
Addressing the first sales clinic of the maritime wholesale hardware association, Dr. MacKinnon said that a "fundamental necessity to the forward march of the Atlantic area economy is "proper use of our land."
"We are wasting much of this valuable asset- 2,500 vacant farms on Prince Edward Island alone. Agriculture is a basic industry upon which every other industry depends, and agriculture is changing. It is not too much to say that in 10 years most present-day farm methods will be obsolete. What are we doing about it?"
The APEC president stated that he had not heard "any good reason why a good living can't be made off a farm and why all our vacant land cannot be taken up again and utilized to the full with profit.
There is no sense in being short-sighted in agriculture; it demands careful planning and the same emphasis on giving the consumer a high quality product that has worked well in industry. Artificial, temporary aids like floor prices are good in only a limited way.
Hard facts must be faced; for example, if the Texans can sell their carrots effectively in our own stores when we are growing them here and cannot sell them, we simply have to learn how to grow and sell carrots properly.
There is gold in the grass right here, too, but we need nothing short of a complete revolution in farm methods to get it."
We shall await with great interest the introduction of the government's legislation

The Address-Mr. Michaud as it will apply to the vital question of credit assistance to agriculture.
Much has been said lately, Mr. Speaker, in regard to certain fishing practices in the maritimes. Needless to say this is of the greatest concern to all those interested in the future welfare of our fisheries, particularly the lobster industry. Many suggestions were offered as to the best methods to stop those poaching practices which seem to be common around some of our shores. The debating point centres on two main suggestions: more education, or more rigidity on the part of conservation officers. I would respectfully submit that both are essential. I recall with satisfaction a series of lectures held in my own constituency in the early summer of 1954. I remain convinced that those lectures, by and large, were beneficial, and my only criticism at this time is that such a program, or other programs of a similar nature, was not further pursued.
We were told that the fisheries department has in its possession films on various aspects of lobster fishing, the life history and the habits of this fish. I am sure that great benefits could be derived if those films were shown in every fishing community. Pamphlets on these same matters could also be distributed in schools, which the school children would subsequently bring back to their homes.
However, Mr. Speaker, despite all efforts to convince fishermen that those illegal practices are detrimental to the good of the industry and to their own personal good, we must be realistic enough to recognize that poaching is an evil that will still remain with us. This is where the department, through its protective staff, will have to intervene with the appropriate measures to master the situation. The best-intentioned fishermen, and those are surely by far the larger number, are demanding action by the department; for many are now convinced that unless a halt is put to the present scale of poaching practices the whole future of the lobster industry will be imperilled.
As an indication of the organized fishermen's views-and these are essentially wellmeaning fishermen-I should like at this time to quote from a news item which I read in the Moncton Times dated January 24 last, containing some of the recommendations made during a recent meeting held in Shediac, New Brunswick, in connection with fishing regulations. I am not commenting on the adequacy of these recommendations; I am simply quoting them as an indication of the trend of thought among the fishing people on this matter:
1. That any fisherman found with illegal lobsters in his possession be required to pay a minimum fine of $2 for each illegal lobster.

2. That any fisherman found with more than 50 per cent illegal lobsters in his possession be subject to the minimum fine of $2 for each illegal lobster, plus the suspension of licence for a 12-month period.
The news item adds:
All fishermen present were in agreement that a strict adherence to the regulations would tend to bring the industry to a higher level, and be a distinct advantage to all concerned.
The general consciousness of all those concerned with this vital matter, Mr. Speaker, augurs well for its ultimate solution.

Mr. Speaker, you must be an innately modest man to be able to withstand the wealth of compliments handed to you in the past two weeks, but at the risk of overdoing it I am going to add my own. Also, Mr. Speaker, may I add my voice to the voices of all other members on both the government and opposition sides in complimenting the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) on the masterly performance of each.
I have, if I may say so at this time, a matter to refer to which perhaps has not been debated so far, namely the royal commission on energy resources. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that there seems to be a misconception of the role of royal commissions. Royal commissions are to collect facts and make recommendations. The government may or may not accept them. Sometimes it accepts them	in full,	sometimes in part	and sometimes	not	at	all.	It is a grand	thing that
under our democratic system the government makes the final decision, as the government will doubtless do in this case.
So	far	as	the	recommendations of thatcommission are concerned, may I simply say that for my part I cannot help but be glad	that	it	has	recommended	a national
energy board, provided, however, that such energy board is not so restrictive and so final as to throttle that very energetic industry, the oil and gas industry. On the other recommendation, which may or may not be the correct interpretation, I for one must object to the suggestion that the energy board should attempt to limit the profits on equity capital, to what they consider a fair amount; because to do that, Mr. Speaker, without including in the decision the whole picture, would be to throttle the expansion which is going on at the present time and would bring an end to the risk capital without which the tremendous strides in the Canadian west in oil and gas production could not possibly have been made.
Having said that, may I say at this time- and I have not had an opportunity to do it before-that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), in his references to the

Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), was wistful. At this stage may I say that I would like to be nostalgic, just for a moment, because it is not so many years ago that I sat at the feet of a certain history professor at the University of Toronto called Pearson, Mike Pearson. We did not know then that his name was Lester. In those days, as we had those quiet seances in his chambers in Baldwin Hall, many of us wondered what he would become, whether he would be a great history professor or whether he would be a great football coach. I suppose he had that problem to decide himself. None of us, however, suspected-least of all I-that my old history professor would one day occupy the second most important position in this chamber, that of leader of Her Majesty's opposition. I want to compliment him at this time upon his achievement.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I should say that no one could have been more amazed than I at the opening of the throne speech debate to see my old history professor, so kindly, so good-natured and so charming as he was then, come out of his corner of the ring fighting, swinging in all directions. He kept on doing that for an hour and a half, and I thought he certainly had changed. After that hour and a half the good humour we all know he possesses asserted itself, and for the next hour he made his points, yes, but he made them with a smile on his face as if to say, "Well, boys, I have to say this but does it not sound ridiculous?" I know he will not mind me saying this, because I know he has a sense of humour.
I went home over the weekend, Mr. Speaker, just to go from home to home in my riding of Rosedale, which includes such parts of Toronto as Regent Park and Cab-bagetown mentioned so eloquently by the hon. member for Port Arthur, and I was somewhat amazed to find that the people there were really fed up with the debate so far. They felt that the government had been criticized, and it should be criticized, but that the criticism was of the carping, destructive type. They felt it was time the opposition parties became constructive in their criticism. I came back to the house prepared to say something about it, but I did not need to because on Monday night last the Leader of the Opposition realized the disservice that his party was doing not only to itself but to the country. Having realized this, he rose in the house and suggested that the throne speech debate be brought to an end, and quite properly so under all the circumstances.
Perhaps in the future, Mr. Speaker, we can have some constructive criticism in the throne speech debate. I would suggest also
The Address-Mr. Walker that we should consider the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition and perhaps in future years reduce the duration of the throne speech debate from ten days to five. Surely all that needs to be said could be said in five days instead of the present ten.
I was surprised also to learn that my friend the Leader of the Opposition had visited Montreal over the weekend, during which time he had made a speech. According to the report I read in the Globe and Mail he made this statement:
It is obvious that something is going to blow.
He was not talking about a football team, and he was not talking about himself. He added:
The government is sitting on an inflationary time bomb.
I should like to ask the hon. gentleman, my former professor: which horse are you on, inflation or unemployment? Unlike the rider in the circus, the Leader of the Opposition cannot ride both horses at the same time because they go in opposite directions. I ask him, as the Prime Minister asked him at the opening of the debate, where does he stand in connection with the situation which confronts Canada today? In his opinion, which has priority,-unemployment or inflation?
We have heard a great deal from the members of the opposition-able speeches they were-on the subject of the deficit. All sorts of figures have been suggested, and some of them are fantastic figures. None of these figures has been more fantastic than the one which came from the newly incorporated Martin bureau of imaginative statistics, which set the deficit at over a billion dollars. This is a gross exaggeration, of course; but supposing the deficit is, as has been suggested, $700 million. Has the government no authority, has the government no support, has the government nothing outside of its own decision to support a deficit of that kind? I ask you that. The opposition members apparently think not.
May I remind them that the Leader of the Opposition himself has justified the position in which the government finds itself today in its deficit budgeting by a speech which he made on February 10 last, or which is reported in the Toronto Daily Star of February 10 last. At that time he was campaigning to become prime minister. The article states:
Hon. Lester Pearson today promised the Canadian people a program of major tax cuts and social changes if the Liberals were returned to power on March 31. He pledged tax reductions of $400 million to spur the lagging economy.
Then the article goes on:
The $400 million tax cut proposed by Mr. Pearson would add to the budget deficit for the coming fiscal
478	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Walker year which his colleague, Hon. George Marler, has estimated will come to around $380 million as a result of existing commitments.
On that basis, if Mr. Pearson's program was put into effect during the next session, the federal government would end the 1958-59 fiscal year with a deficit in the neighbourhood of $800 million-
Now, that is the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition himself, made when he was campaigning for election; yet now his supporters have castigated the government for having the deficit which it is expected they might have. I do not know that he has pressed such views with vigour, but his supporters have. Then according to this article he went even further:
If the situation deteriorated still further, Mr. Pearson stated that he was prepared to recommend even greater deficit financing.
Think of it, Mr. Speaker; here he is on record on February 10 last, and contrast that with the speeches we have heard in this house since that time. Then the Leader of the Opposition went on to boast about the Liberal party, and the article reads:
Mr. Pearson said the idea of creating a budget deficit was in keeping with principles of the Liberal party which had reduced the national debt by $2,500 million during the prosperous post-war years, while resorting to deficit financing in 1955 when that was necessary to stimulate the economy.
What we find is this, and I have figures here to prove it; that the Liberals talk about cyclical budgeting as if they had invented it, yet in the recession years of 1954 and 1957 they budgeted for a surplus. When we came into power in 1957 the Liberals had budgeted for a surplus in that year of recession, while in the boom years 1955 and 1956 they contrived to have deficits. The theory of cyclical budgeting is to reduce demand when it is excessive and inflation threatens, and to expand demand when it is deficient and unemployment is the major item. However, far from reducing the amplitude of the economic fluctuations during the last cycle between 1954 and 1957, the Liberals actually increased those fluctuations. On the basis of their figures they had surpluses when they should have had deficits and they had deficits when they should have had surpluses. The figures speak for themselves.
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the speech of the Leader of the Opposition in Montreal may I say this. The facts would appear to indicate otherwise than the likelihood of this time bomb going off at the present time or in the near future; because it would appear that the inflationary tendency which has been in evidence in recent months is almost at an end and that the year 1959 will be a year of renewed expansion, with increased stability of prices. Such inflation as we have had since


assuming office is not "demand" inflation. It is not what we used to call classical inflation. It is not that at all; it could not possibly be so because there is no pressure upon our resources. No one knows better than does the Leader of the Opposition that the tremendous influx of capital investment in our country since the war has begun to assert itself in the great capacity of this country for production. This result is already instanced by the fact that the commodity price structure has at last become stabilized. As a matter of fact we have now more stability in commodity prices than we have had in years.
Therefore, with the greatest of respect to the Leader of the Opposition, I ask whether it is not wrong that he should stress this "demand" inflation over the immediate and pressing problem of unemployment. It seems to be generally accepted by economists that in 1959 the level of prices possibly will rise a little, and that the only reason that prices will rise at all will be cost factors such as, for instance, increased freight rates, increased wages and matters of that kind. After all- and this is fundamental in answering the Leader of the Opposition-the theory of supply and demand is still extant, and there is no possibility of a runaway inflation such as that about which he has the people worried. Furthermore, and credit for this is due to our Minister of Finance, the government of Canada and the Bank of Canada have carefully kept a firm check on the supply of money, not permitting it to go up in recent months. This fact is extremely important.
I do not know what happened to the Leader of the Opposition last week end when he went to Montreal. It may be that he visited some of the boys on St. James street with his old friend Mr. Howe, who may have introduced him to some of his colleagues on the 40 or more directorates of which he is a distinguished member. I do not know what it was that happened, but in any event the Leader of the Opposition made this speech about the fear that something was going to blow imminently. May I say to him with the greatest respect-and he knows I have for him the greatest respect-that to quote the words of the late President Roosevelt, "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself."
All we have to fear is fear which might lead to what is known as a psychological inflation. If these prophets of doom and gloom or, as the Prime Minister has called them, the gloomsters, led by the Leader of the Opposition, continue to pound away on the theme that inflation is inevitable, then in time by the very repetition of this thought, they may convince the consumer and the businessman himself that perhaps after all

there is no use in resisting increased prices, that perhaps after all inflation is inevitable. That is called psychological inflation; and that is possible in this country; but it is only possible if the gloomsters continue to pound away on the subject which I suggest, with great respect, does not have any merit at the present time.
How can we have a runaway inflation at the present time? The facts belie the statement. Here we have commodity futures at a low and world trade depressed. When the economy of our country is operating below capacity not only in Canada but in the United States, how can you have a runaway inflation? How can this bomb go off at the present time? But if the gloomsters continue to pound away, then it may happen.
That would be a catastrophe, Mr. Speaker, because if our costs and prices continue to go up our competitive position both in our domestic market and, what is more important, our export market will be undermined. If that event happens Canada will be exporting jobs to the United States and other countries, Mr. Speaker; and this is one export which we the people of Canada cannot afford.

The Address-Mr. Walker
May my concluding and final point be this. This problem of the communist trade offensive and the vital importance of expanded world markets to the future prosperity of Canada and, as a matter of fact, the rest of the world, were the reason for the Prime Minister's world tour. The Prime Minister and Canadians generally wish to increase economic co-operation between the east and the west-as I am sure do all members of the house-between the developed countries and the undeveloped countries, between those which have and those which have not. If we are effectively to combat this communist trade offensive then we, one of the western countries, with all the other western countries must join with the uncommitted eastern countries and work together for world trade.
That is the message which the Prime Minister took with him around the world. Mr. Speaker, I do not think the people of Canada have any idea what a tremendously successful commonwealth tour the Prime Minister had. I have taken the liberty of going through the press of all the countries of the commonwealth at the time he happened to be there. I should have liked to take the time of the house to tell hon. members-but because there are many others who wish to speak I will not do so-of the tremendous impression made by "Mr. Canada" during that tour. It was fantastic. Wherever he went he brought fresh hope and a new vision of commonwealth solidarity. He has done much, and we all recognize this, to cement the bonds of commonwealth by stressing in particular, and this is very important, the ties of trade. I should like to have gone on with what has been said in the different countries but may I just quote from the newspaper in India known as the Hindu of Madras. That newspaper had this to say:
Mr. Diefenbaker has recently manifested a refreshing freedom from preconceived notions and prejudices. Mr. Diefenbaker reveals himself as a statesman who is interested in seeking remedies for the world's ills which will cure instead of worsening them.
In Australia's Sydney Morning Herald he was praised for "a vigorous and consistent Asian policy with firm aims imaginatively pursued, a condition of survival for this commonwealth." The London Observer summed it all up with these words:
His great success was that he persuaded all those with whom he came into contact that whatever they had thought to the contrary they were fully members of a great fraternity in which they were regarded as good as the next man.
How important it is to convey that message. Finally may I place on the records of the house the greatest tribute of all, delivered by the Prime Minister of Great Britain at the Albert hall meeting when our Prime Minister

The Address-Mr. Peters addressed an overflow audience. This is what the Prime Minister of Great Britain said:
From the first talks we had together X realized that we had here a great man, and great because he had the one vital thing that any great man must have,-faith. He has faith in his fellow countrymen, in the tasks which Canada has to undertake and the contribution she has to make to the whole world. He has faith in the continuing and, indeed, ever-increasing moral and political value of that unique combination of nations which we call the commonwealth; faith as he has told you today, in the economic progress and development of an ever-expanding commonwealth based upon the steady development of industrial power and financial strength and, above all, faith that in the great secular struggle between the principles of freedom and communism the commonwealth can play an immense and, perhaps under providence, a decisive part.
That was the tribute of the Prime Minister of Great Britain. In this connection may I say that in the 19 months since the Conservative government took office commonwealth relations and trade have been stimulated as never before, first by the very successful mission headed by our able Minister of Trade and Commerce to the United Kingdom; second, by the Montreal conference presided over by our distinguished Minister of Finance; and finally by the world tour of the Prime Minister.
In conclusion may I say that it is time we united to boost our country. We are all good Canadians. Everybody in every party on both sides of the house is a good Canadian and none is a better Canadian than the other. But is it not time that we started to talk ourselves up? At the risk of appearing to be sentimental, and I do not feel that way at all, may I paraphrase words of Tennyson:
To Canada, whom we love and prize
Whatever statesman holds the helm;
Hands all round
God the glooms|er's hopes confound;
To this great cause of Canada
Praise,-my friends,
And all her glorious provinces
Round and round.
